utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In one minute before the witness takes the solemn declaration, administrative matters necessary to make the best use of our time. It's obvious that at the present rate of progress we aren't going to be able even to take all the witnesses I think on the schedule. I'm having to make preliminary decisions about which witnesses we may drop, and I will of course be assisted by knowing in due course what prospective cross-examination the accused would want and would be granted in respect of candidates for abbreviation. It may help if I tell the Chamber the following: The witness listed for next Wednesday, Sarinic, is on the list for four hours but that was before the 89(F) ruling was made. We will seek for him to be dealt with in a period of time less than that in toto. And then there are two witnesses -- I don't ask for any indications at the moment. There are two witnesses, General Vegh on the 5th of February, and Mr. Brunborg on the 4th of February, each of whom is experts and against whom substantial periods of time are currently marked. In each case we will be asking for them, if they are taken at all, to be taken more shortly. And were it possible at some stage for the accused and/or the amici to accept, or the Court to rule, that cross-examination need not be too extensive, that would help us. But I hope that these indications of where we are will assist the Court because it would be preferable to plan rather than simply to run out of time, and I want to be able to plan which witnesses properly should be dropped and which should be taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Which are the two witnesses again?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Apart from Sarinic next week, it's General Vegh on the 5th of February and the expert Brunborg on the 4th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Did you say 4th of February?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: 4th of February I think, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Not 28th of January.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He was the 28th and I think he's been moved. Maybe there's a later version, but in any case, he's the expert, Brunborg. That's all, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. If the witness would take the declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you. If you'd take a seat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if we could begin. The Prosecution will be tendering two exhibits; one is the expert report of this witness Dr. Zecevic, and the other is a binder of 30 exhibits. If we could ask that numbers be assigned.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the expert report will be marked Exhibit 636 and the binder of exhibits will be 637.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interests of saving time, the Prosecution wishes to withdraw three exhibits from the binder which is now 637. Those are exhibits -- or tabs 6, 16, and 28. I apologise that the curriculum vitae in tab 1 is also included in the expert report, so the Prosecution will be withdrawing the second copy of that that was included in tab 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to begin your testimony by telling us your full name.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Berko Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And the Chamber has a full record of your education and professional background before it now. Could I ask you to summarise in a sentence or two what your field of expertise is.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I specialised in two fields. Education; that is to say, teaching at the faculty of mechanical engineering, and also my expert work in the field of designing ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time, if it's acceptable to the Court, I will read a summary of what it is that is contained in the expert report and then proceed with my questions regarding some other matters of fact that the witness has information regarding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Have you a copy of that document or is it your own personal summary that you're going to read?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just a summary that I have some speaking notes of that. It's not an official document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: This witness, a mechanical engineer, is a highly qualified expert in heavy weapons technology of the former Yugoslavia, and prior to the war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, he was involved in the design of heavy weapons, including the 120-millimetre mortar for the JNA. During the war, he assisted the Bosnian and Herzegovina government with a weapons production industry. His full statement as an expert pursuant to Rule 94 bis reports on the operation and effect of the 120-millimetre mortar round and the shelling of Markale market in Sarajevo on the 5th of February, 1994. At that time, he had volunteered to participate in the investigation of the shelling of the market and was appointed by the local investigating judge as part of a team of engineers who analysed the physical evidence and prepared a study on the shelling. His analysis concluded, in part, the following: One, that the 120-millimetre mortar round exploded upon impact with the surface of the ground in the market and that the tail stabiliser fin of that mortar was found lodged in the centre of the crater created by the mortar; that his analysis determined that it came from the north north-east direction in an azimuth of 18 degrees plus or minus two degrees. Third, that there were six possible locations from which the shell could have been fired from. Fourth, that of those six locations, only the closest one of those sites was under the control of the government of Bosnia and Herzegovina army at the time. The other five possible locations were in territory controlled by the army of Republika Srpska. Fifth, that UNPROFOR personnel interviewed -- stated that they had not observed a single projectile fired from the area of controlled -- the area controlled by the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina at a time relevant and that it would be impossible to hide the sound of the firing of a 120-millimetre mortar in that area or in that controlled area; therefore concluding that the round must have been fired from one of the other five locations. Six, that it is scientifically possible that one 120-millimetre mortar shell was able to kill the large number of people that it did kill on that day. And finally, that the lack of colour on the tail stabiliser fin as recovered indicates most probably that it was manufactured in the Pretis arms manufacturing plant in Vogosca or Marko Oreskovic in Licki Osik in Croatia, both of which were under the control of the army of Republika Srpska at the relevant time. This expert also reports upon and explains scientific research that indicates that the tail stabiliser fin of the Yugoslav 120-millimetre mortar round would not begin to lodge into the ground if fired on charges 1 and 2 and that it would be unlikely to lodge if fired with three charges and would begin to lodge if fired with four, five, or six charges. On the basis of this research, it can be concluded, or he has concluded, that the round was fired from Bosnian Serb-controlled territory. Your Honour, I will now ask the witness regarding matters relevant to his time working in the Pretis factory.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you to summarise the number of years that you worked in the Pretis factory.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I worked there for 17 years.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And during the time that you were there, did you become familiar with the paperwork of the Pretis factory as well as correspondence that regularly transpired between Pretis, other munitions factories, and the JNA?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was in the department for research and development of the Pretis factory. That is actually the nucleus in terms of the operation of that factory. That is to say manufacturing ammunition. There were 30 to 50 of us employed in that department, depending on the year, and of course we all had the opportunity of seeing how our colleagues developed. The most responsible people for designing, testing, and introducing ammunition in the Yugoslav People's Army were us, and of course we were present in the manufacturing phase, in the testing and experimental stage, and since this was our very own country at the time, we were all pleased if we could help the Yugoslav People's Army as much as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you specifically regarding the paperwork that was generated typically by the Pretis factory as well as written correspondence between it and the Yugoslav People's Army and other munitions factories. During the course of your employment there, did you become familiar with such documents?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Since I was one of the constructors of the 128-millimetre rocket M87, I went through all stages of its design and its introduction in the Yugoslav People's Army, so it was only logical that I had to be --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Just in the interest of time, if you're able to answer yes or no, I would appreciate that. Were you familiar with the documents?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, yes, yes, fully. Fully.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Over the course of the last several days were you asked to look at some documents from the Pretis factory?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask at this time, if it pleases the Court, that the binder, 637, be placed before the witness so that he can tab through the large number of documents I will ask him to comment on during the course of his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We'll get a number for that.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 637, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you -- can I ask you to turn to tab 2 of that binder, and my question to you: Is that a summary of your observations regarding the documents that you were asked to look at while here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Before I ask you about any specific document, can I ask you in a few sentences to describe for the Chamber what was the pre-war structure of the munitions and weapons industry in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The military industry of the Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia was very well organised with clear competences of all the participants involved. In the process of designing, there were two possibilities; it was done either by the Military Technological Institute in Belgrade or by individual factories. Ammunitions factories were mostly located in Bosnia-Herzegovina and Serbia. Ammunition was tested in Nikinci in Serbia. Decisions on whether anything should be developed in the field of ammunition was passed by the Military Technical Council of the Yugoslav People's Army, the -- such a decision would be adopted by the council too, and the technical division of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence passed the further relevant decisions, and therefore, all the competences were clearly outlined. I have to point out one more thing: For a long time, the rule was that there would be a clear division in terms of what each factory should do. For a long time, there had been no parallelism in production. It appeared only towards the very end, towards the 1980s. Before that, the entire organisation was at a very high level. Foreign trade was conducted by the SDPR. The factories themselves did not have the right to sell their products on their own.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe for us, what was the significance of the Pretis factory itself? How large a factory and what quantity of munitions did it produce?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The backbone of any army are the artillery units in addition to infantry units, but the main strikes are carried out by the artillery units. The Pretis factory produced artillery ammunition from 76 millimetres to 155 millimetres, rocket ammunition of 128 millimetres, air bombs of 250 millimetres. So this was a highly respectable factory, perhaps among the largest such factories in Europe for the manufacturing of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness kindly be asked to speak slower.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir -- Doctor, the interpreters are asking if you could speak little bit slower. Doctor, the Chamber has heard evidence about the withdrawal --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: -- of the Yugoslav People's Army from Bosnia-Herzegovina on the 19th of May, 1992. Did you discover a document dated after that time which indicated to you an ongoing relationship between the Yugoslav army, as it was then called, and the Pretis factory? And I'd ask you to turn to tab 3.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And if I could ask that the first page of that document be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise the document that's contained in 637, tab 3?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Was that a document that you yourself located or found?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you summarise for the Chamber what is it is that is stated in that document.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, the president of the Community of Military Industries of Yugoslavia, Mr. Jovan Jovicic, proposes that directors be appointed for various factories, namely Rudi Cajavec, Pretis, and Famos, special vehicles. All of these factories at that time were under the control of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And what does this document purport to do?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was customary in the former Yugoslavia that the appointment of directors would be carried out or, rather, agreement would be sought from the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, although it was the workers' council that actually carried out the appointment. However, not a single case was registered of appointing a director within the military industry without having consulted the Federal Secretariat for National Defence beforehand and without receiving their agreement. In this particular case, objectively speaking, Bosnia-Herzegovina had attained independence, so it would have been illogical to have this done by the then-Federal Secretariat for National Defence. At that point in time, this was proposed by an organisation that still operated, and that was the Community of the Military Industries of Yugoslavia, and it was headed by its president, Jovan Jovicic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, does this document, through the mechanism you've just described, propose a candidate to be the manager of the Pretis factory?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And who does it propose should be the manager of the Pretis factory now located -- or located in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milorad Motika, with a degree in engineering, was proposed to be director of the Pretis factory. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I now ask that you look at tab 4 of 637 and ask that page 1 of the English copy of that document be placed on the overhead projector. Sir, this is a document dated the 18th of June, 1992. Can I ask you to summarise what this document is and can I ask you also to read the conclusion or finding under Roman numeral I.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Under Roman numeral I problems are spelled out because -- those problems were due to the fact that there was a conflict in the territory of Bosnia-Herzegovina and also --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you. Are you sure that you're looking at tab number 4? I believe you're referring to tab number 5 at the moment.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I am sorry. Tab 4. This refers to the appointment of the manager of the Vogosca Pretis holding. Jovo Vucic, the previous manager, was dismissed and Milorad Motika, with a degree in engineering, was appointed manager of the Vogosca Pretis holding, and this was signed by Prime Minister, Professor Dr. Branko Djeric.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Does this indicate that the recommendation for general manager of Pretis, made through the mechanism of the Federal Secretariat, was adopted by the management or by the Pretis -- or was it enacted for the Pretis factory?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the question put by Mr. Groome is unfair because he said the proposal was made through the Federal Secretariat, and this is no proposal of the Federal Secretariat. This is a proposal of a business association that is called the Community of Military Industries and the Manufacturers of Military Equipment. This had existed for years in Yugoslavia. It consisted of the managers of military industry factories. So it has nothing to do with the government, and therefore Mr. Groome is putting a question that is quite wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let us have it clarified.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I ask you to clarify, what was the relationship between the organisation that authored this document that's in tab 3 and the federal organs having to do with the military in Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The fact that the Military Industries Community for Yugoslavia existed several years and that it had been established with a view to resolving some of the common problems in the functioning of the military industry, and it served the following purpose: When exports were made, then joint positions were taken. However, it was not customary for this business community to propose its head. It was always the Federal Secretariat for National Defence that gave its approval. Also the appointment of this director could not have been made on the basis of an independent decision. It wasn't that the managers would meet and appoint another manager. This had to go through the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. My opinion is, if I can put it that way, that at this point in time, it was illogical for the Federal Secretariat for National Defence to put forth a proposal again. So use was made of this community which still existed, and they proposed Mr. Motika to be the general manager. My opinion is there was no synchronisation in this process as there had been before.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I want to draw your attention to April 1992. During that month did you cease to work at the Pretis factory?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on the 17th of April I stopped working there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to briefly describe why it was you stopped working on the 17th of April in 1992?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the days before, there was great tension and shooting in the area of Sarajevo. That week, factories resumed their work, and on that day I came to the factory with a very small number of other colleagues because I thought it impossible for a conflict to break out in Bosnia and Herzegovina, so I came to work in the morning, to the factory. It was around noon or 1.00 p.m., and all of a sudden there was complete silence. This big complex, this factory, employed every day several thousand people, and there was always hum and noise and you could feel it working. However, this was complete silence. And looking through the window of my office, I saw people leaving the factory en masse. I remained there for another couple of hours, and at a certain point I left my office because nobody, none of my colleagues arrived to work that day, although the R&D department was the most important one in the whole factory. There was no director, no senior staff. Nobody was there. Then I left the factory and a couple of days later it was impossible to go in the factory anywhere -- anyway because the JNA had entered the complex.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I can now draw your attention to after the conflict did in fact begin. Can I ask you to summarise for the Chamber the situation with respect to munitions that would have been faced by the early army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The Pretis factory had in its production programme a continuous process. At all times it was producing a significant amount of ammunition. It is a huge complex and part of its storage facilities were used for storing the reserves of the Yugoslav People's Army. It contained a lot of semi-finished products, not ready-made weapons but parts of assemblies that can easily be put together. The stockpile was enough for about five or six months of production.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you perhaps to simply list what, if any, problems the munitions industry at that time in the Republika Srpska would have faced.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can say what problems -- what were the potential problems in Pretis in Republika Srpska, because it was the main factory in that area. First of all, there was the problem of supply with energy, power, supply of steam and coal, because that was necessary for the production. And since the military industry was a unified body, no single factory could work alone so that the factory of rockets and rocket fuels in Vitez was under the control of HVO at the moment. The factory of igniting devices in Bugojno was under the control of HVO, and that created significant problems in putting together the production. And then also there occurred problems in providing inputs for the production of ammunition.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, could I ask you now to turn to tab 5 of 637. This is a document entitled -- it's from the Republika Srpska Ministry of Industry Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. and Energetics, and it's titled information on current problems of military industry of the Republika Srpska, and it's dated the 26th of November, 1992. Have you had an opportunity to review this document, and does it fairly and accurately represent some of the problems that would have been faced by the military and munitions suppliers in the Republika Srpska during this early part of the war?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have seen this document, and I agree completely that this is a realistic assessment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm now going to ask you to turn to tab 7 of 637. You made some mention of raw materials. Can I ask you to describe in a little greater detail what types of materials did the Pretis factory depend on that would become -- or did become unavailable in the latter part of 1992 and continuing on into 1993?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the production of ammunition, there is a series of raw materials that are necessary. One of the important components is steel that was supplied from Slovenia, Croatia, or from Niksic and Zenica, which means Bosnia-Herzegovina. Furthermore, rocket fuels for rocket artillery systems are very important as well. Such fuels could be supplied from the Vitez factory, which was then under the control of HVO, or from the Lucani factory in Serbia. I have to emphasise that fuels from the Vitez and Lucani factories were not compatible but were used for only certain types of ammunition. A special problem were fuses and capsules for the production of cartridges. One needs brass. Copper is needed from Serbia. And bearing in mind the overall situation, production in Pretis was made very difficult unless we could complete the supply of all the inputs.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Explosives were a special problem. They were also supplied from Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, I asking you to draw your attention to the tab 7 of 637. This is a document dated the 20th of September, 1994, and it's signed by Mr. Motika, the director of the Pretis company. Does this document describe the types of munitions that are being produced in 1994, and does it summarise the situation in 1994 with respect to the supply of the raw materials necessary for their production?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This enumerates practically the entire span of Pretis's production before and during the war, and this overview specifies the factories which supplied raw materials to our factory, indicating the current problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And according to this document, have some or many of the problems that existed in 1992 been resolved at this stage in November 1994?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could now draw your attention to tab 8 of 637 and ask that the first page of the English translation be placed on the overhead projector. This is a document dated the 6th of November, 1992, signed once again by Mr. Motika. Can I ask you to summarise in a sentence or two what it is that this document is referring to.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is a communication between two factories, one being Pretis from Vogosca, Sarajevo, and the factory of Lucani. And the subject of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. this letter is production of projectiles for a 125-millimetre tank, M84. The factory in Blagovici produces ammunition for this weapon and produces fuel for this weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Could I ask you to now look at tab 9 of 637 and once again ask that the first page be placed on the overhead projector. This is a document dated the 11th of August, 1995. Can I ask you to describe what is contained in this document.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, Mr. Milorad Motika requests from the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska to secure the transport into Republika Srpska from Republika Srpska -- from the Republic of Serbia TNT in the amount of 12.000 kilos and copper tubing in the amount of 8.000 kilos.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, during this time period were there agreements or barter agreements where raw materials and partially finished products were traded between the factories that now existed in the Republika Srpska and factories that existed in the Republic of Serbia itself?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think it would have been a natural effort, because they would not have been able to function one without the other, just as today factories that belong to the military industry in various territories are trying to establish cooperation. It is a natural way out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at tab 10 of 637. That's a contract dated the 24th of July, 1995. Is that one such example of a barter agreement?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Then if you would please look at tab 11. It's a document dated the 10th of November, 1992, once again signed by Mr. Motika. Is this -- does this document also indicate the existence of an agreement to barter materials?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I could not say that this document speaks of -- speaks to barter agreements. This document reflects the request of Mr. Motika, addressed to the Institute for Technical Repairs, which is an organisation of the Yugoslav army, to supply a certain amount of elements needed for the production of ammunition -- or, rather, I'm sorry, I'm sorry. I didn't notice at first the second page. It does reflect exactly what you said. Both these documents reflect barter deals. I did not pay attention at first to the heading.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And finally, could I ask you to look at 637, tab 12, and ask you to comment on this document and what it says.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this document the Krusik factory from Valjevo, Serbia, sells fuses TK-M71 and AU-18 as well as ammunition M74 to the Pretis factory with the price being fixed by one of the departments of the Secretariat for National Defence. These are the most important elements of this communication, this document, I would say. And that ties in with what I said before, namely that the Federal Secretariat, even before the war, would make estimates of the value of an hour of work, an hour of labour, or the price of a certain type of ammunition on the market.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If I could now draw your attention to tab 13 of 637. Is this one of the documents that you were asked to review here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And my question to you with respect to this document is: Does this document indicate that the Republika Srpska Ministry of Defence was directly involved itself in some of these barter agreements?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, if I could ask you to please turn to 14 of Exhibit 637 and ask that the first page be placed on the overhead projector. Have you had an opportunity to review this document; and if so, can you please describe what this document indicates? And this is a document dated the 29th of January, 1994.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I did have occasion to review it. In this document, the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, the logistics sector, informs via the Ministry of Defence of Republika Srpska, informs the Pretis factory that it is unable to provide 2.000 tons of steel from the Niksic steel works, needed for normal operation, due to lack of funds. And at the same time, they emphasise that in the process of securing 100 tons of explosives in exchange for 125-millimetre ammunition for M84 tanks, it was approved, and that we see in item 3, that the Krusik enterprise would provide mines for the Pretis factory, mortar shells in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I draw your attention to the first sentence under the CC where it says: "Notification on the allocation of technical equipment and material by the Yugoslav army." Do you see that portion?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a minute, please. I can't see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to check the tab at the front of the document. It's the number at the front of the document.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Tab 14 you say?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. I'll move on and perhaps look at your binder during the break. I want to now ask you to turn your attention to tab number 15. Could I ask that the original -- a copy of the original be given to the witness so he can check that it is the same one that's in his binder, and could I please ask that the English be placed on the ELMO. Sir, to ensure that there's been no confusion or mix-up in your binder, could I ask you to just compare what you have in your binder as tab 15 with the three -- with the pages that are to you right now? Are they the same?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe what this document is.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, director Milorad Motika is addressing a request to General Mladic at the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, asking him to urge the chief of General Staff of the army of Yugoslav, General Perisic, to make sure that 1.000 pieces of rocket engines of 122-millimetre rocket engines be forwarded to Krusik Holding in Valjevo to meet the needs of Pretis Holding, and to do this through the assistant Defence Minister of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interests of time, the Prosecution is withdrawing tab 16 of this exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, you've been discussing Pretis and its manufacturing capacity during the period of 1992 to 1995. In the documents that you were asked to examine here in The Hague, did you find indications of where a large number of the munitions that were produced were eventually sent from the Pretis factory?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: You mean during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The largest part of that ammunition was used in the theatre of operations around Sarajevo by the army of Republika Srpska, namely the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: During the war, because of your expertise, were you called upon to sometimes visit the scenes of where shells had landed in the city of Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was involved twice, the first time when there was an explosion in the Markale market, and the second time when a rocket projectile was fired on the Sarajevo television.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you ever come to know from your personal knowledge that shells bearing a manufacturing date of 1993 had been discovered in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At that time, I was still head of the research and development sector attached to the Main Staff, and one of my responsibilities was to find an alternative way of supply, and among the detected unexploded shells was a shell with a manufacturing date of 1993. It was produced in the Krusik factory in Valjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where are those two factories located, in what republic?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That factory is located in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: So within the city of Sarajevo, you found an unexploded shell that had been manufactured in 1993 in Serbia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to now ask you to look at the document in 637, tab 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to ask that page number 7 of that -- of the English version of that be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My apologies; tab 17, page 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: My question to you is: This document dated 11th of February, 1993, does it include an accounting of where some of the munitions produced at Pretis were sent, to what units of the army of Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I know that you do read some English. Can I ask you to take the pointer and point to the column on the English version of that document on the overhead projector to your left. Can I ask you to point to the columns that refer to munitions. And you need to do it on the original at your left hand.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [In English] Uh-huh, okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can you point to the columns that indicate the munitions that were sent to units involved in the Sarajevo area.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Column 4, column 5, column 6, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 15, 18, 19, 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. Can I now turn your attention to tab 18 of 637. This is a report dated 5th of December, 1993. My question to you is: Does it indicate the amounts of ammunition supplied between the 1st of January, 1993 and the 30th of November, 1993?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you would now please turn to tab 19 of 637. This is a document dated the 6th of July, 1995. Can I ask you to summarise what is contained in this document. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, the logistical sector of the technological department of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska addresses a request to the Pretis factory, to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps command, and to the forward command post of SRK to deliver certain ammunition including 100-millimetre, 105-millimetre, 122-millimetre mortar shells, the previous two rounds, and in the fourth position 122-millimetre rounds.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: If you would now turn to tab 20 of 637. If I could ask you to describe what is contained in that document.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, which is certified by the seal of the Pretis factory, we see a list of certain amounts of ammunition that was delivered to various brigades active in the area of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I will withdraw, in the interests of time, tab 21. If I could ask you to turn to tab 22 of 637. And I ask that the first page of the English be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, does this document, entitled a "Review of the ammunition, explosive ordnance and other armament and military equipment delivered for the period of the 1st of January to the 31st of September, 1993," does it indicate the total quantity in percentage of the output of the Pretis factory that was forwarded to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Out of the total quantity, 67.3 per cent was delivered to the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Now, based upon your experience, were you -- were there some types of armaments that could only be produced in the Republic of Serbia itself?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All guided means were produced in Republic of Serbia; mortar shells, 120, 122, and 60-millimetre; ammunition for anti-air guns; ammunition for infantry weapons. That is what I know. And probably some more complicated systems that may have started to be developed during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm going to now turn your attention to tab 23 of 637. And I ask you what is indicated by this document, the document dated the 30th of March, 1993.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, the technical testing centre in Nikinci, this document, which is addressed by the director of the control of the Pretis enterprise, request is made to test five 125-millimetre projectiles for the -- for two tanks, T72 and M82. This is a standard process. When a certain number of ammunition has been manufactured, a certain number of samples be selected to be tested in the technical testing centre, and if the ammunition corresponds to the standards set, then that ammunition is delivered to the units.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And where is this testing centre located?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The testing centre is in Nikinci, which is close to Sabac, the town of Sabac in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Would you now please turn your attention to tab 24 of 637, and I ask that the first page of the English be placed on the overhead projector. This is document dated the 21st of May, 1994, also signed by Mr. Motika. Does this document also indicate that some munitions were sent to Nikinci for testing?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It says here that two modified 128-millimetre M63 rockets are being sent to the technical testing centre in Nikinci. In this case signed by the Pretis Holding manager, Milorad Motika.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm finished with that document. Sir, I'm now going to ask that you turn your attention to the topic of fuel air explosives. Are you familiar with what that munition is; and if so, briefly describe what it is for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Air explosives, or thermobaric, or full air explosives are explosives that we used in the Vietnam War, in Chechnya, and these are devices for massive destruction of a certain region. They don't affect the individual targets but they affect the whole surface, and by their effects they have greater consequences regarding manpower and light armoured vehicles than when using solid explosives. Their effect is particularly dangerous in closed areas and urban centres when there are -- when there is a considerable increase in the effect of the explosives. These explosives were developed for the air force in the 1980s. And in the Pretis factory before the war, we were about to complete the development of a 250-millimetre bomb filled with this explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, did you recently obtain a photograph of such bombs that were deployed by the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask that tab 30 of 637 be placed on the overhead projector.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to describe what it is we're looking at and just generally about this type of bomb.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This couldn't really be called a bomb. It's a rocket projectile which contains a warhead equivalent to a 250-kilogramme bomb. This projectile consists of three rocket engines, a warhead, which is the body of the air bomb, 250, and a stabilising fin attached to the back part of the rocket engine. This is a relatively simple manufacture of a Russian system which consisted of four racket engines used close to Sarajevo in 1994. This rocket system is not precise, but what I did have occasion to analyse during the use of one such system against TV Sarajevo building, it has a very considerable destructive effect. Within the warhead there is liquid explosive, propylene oxide, and the solid explosive is inside and its task is to destroy the body. The fuse at the tip, upon impact, it penetrates the obstacle and with a delay of four, seven, or 15 seconds, it activates the cover, the cartridge, the liquid evaporates, mixes with air, and an explosion occurs, and the whole system has a blast effect on the surroundings.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can I now ask you to look at tabs 25 -- look at 25 first and just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Where was this picture taken, the picture of this bomb?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Dr. Zecevic, do you know where this picture was taken?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I couldn't really tell you, but I know who took the picture. This photograph in this form -- or, rather, the appearance of this projectile I didn't have occasion to see until this photograph was obtained, because on the spot when it was used against the television building, I only found the rocket engines with the stabiliser. The warhead had exploded, so I Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. couldn't find it in its original form but only parts of it. A year and a half ago I had occasion to meet with a Dutch officer who was in charge in Bosnia for -- of efforts to find unexploded ammunitions, and during a conversation, I asked him whether he had occasion to come across such a system. And he said that he did several times, and then he sent me these photographs. I'm afraid I don't know his name, but I do have his visiting card, and I can provide it for you. He also has photographs of Russian systems that -- on which this system was modelled. So such examples were found in Bosnia-Herzegovina in unexploded form.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you to turn your attention to tab 25 of 637, and if you would just in a sentence or two describe what it is that is indicated by this document dated the 16th of June, 1995.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In this document, the logistics sector of the technical department of the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska is addressing to the command of the 35th logistics base and of the 27th logistic base and the Pretis factory an announcement that the 35th base will transport to Pretis aerial bombs, FAB100 kilogrammes, 15 pieces of 250 kilogrammes, I think it says here 14 or 11 pieces, and rocket engines of 128-millimetres, 57 pieces, which will be completed, 500 with one engine each --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Can I ask you just in the interest of time, can I ask you to look at tab 26 of 637. Is that also some correspondence with respect to Pretis and these fuel or explosives?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Very similar. Very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And once again, to tab number 27?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, very similar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The motors for some of these bombs, where did they come from in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In view of the fact that Pretis was unable to get hold of rocket fuel, it could no longer manufacture 128-millimetre rockets that were standard, nor could it obtain fuel for 122-millimetre rockets which it started to develop just before the war. These had to be imported, which means purchased abroad and then transported to Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And based on your experience, what avenues would have been used for the purchase of such necessary components?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Normally they could be purchased in Romania, Bulgaria, Russia, Belarussia. In June 1993, a platoon started acting on the urban part of Sarajevo, and I was close to the point of impact. I went there and found parts of rocket motors with inscriptions indicating repair institute -- technical repair institute Kragujevac, and the year was 1991. Later on when TV Sarajevo was shelled, I also saw engines with inscriptions indicating that those 122-millimetre rockets were prepared in the technical repair institute in Kragujevac in Serbia. And in my report, you can find photographs of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: After Serb forces left Vogosca in the Sarajevo area in February 1996, did you find drawings related to the launching of such bombs or such rockets?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were some designs for the launching devices for such systems.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just had a chance to look at them.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Without going into the technical details of these launching systems, were you able to determine where these drawings were created and at what time they were created?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It said VTI on them, Military Technical Institute of the ground forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And that would have been from what republic?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Bosnia and Herzegovina. You mean the Military Technical Institute?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The drawings that you discovered that had to do with launching, methods on how to launch these rockets, what are you able to tell us about who authored them and at what time they were authored?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They were authored by the Military Technical Institute in Belgrade. When, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, in the interests of time I will not play an intercept, which is now Exhibit 613, intercept number 244, but I would draw the Chamber's attention to it in relation to the next question that I'll ask the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Sir, can you -- how were these bombs commonly referred to during this time period?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They were known as FAB 100 or FAB 250. The first weighed 100 kilogrammes and FAB 250 indicated 250 kilogrammes, so the code number indicates the weight of the air bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: How long -- I don't think you've said anything so far, have you, as to how long you were going to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, about this examination?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, your examination. I don't think we had any discussion about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Not with myself, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: No, and I don't think as far as anybody's concerned, but obviously we must recognise the time which is available, and at the same time, of course, it must be a fair examination. Have you any other matters you have to deal with today, the Prosecution, for instance?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I know that Mr. Tieger is anxious to resume the cross-examination and, if possible, complete that today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. We've considered coming to a fair decision as far as the ability which the accused must have to be able to present his case in cross-examination, at the same time, having regard to all parties. What we will do is this; that we will allow the rest of the day for

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: time, to allow the amicus to ask some questions if that's going to be possible. So, Mr. Milosevic, start, make a start.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. May. I really do wish, first of all, to thank Mr. Groome for bringing such a witness here, and especially for producing so many documents. And now, after two years, we can see in this courtroom the enormous quantity of ammunition that was manufactured in the territory of the former Bosnia and Herzegovina, including Republika Srpska, and it can even be seen that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia or, rather, the army of Yugoslavia purchased certain devices and ammunition there. Until here, it was -- the prevalent view was that everything came from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It's not time for speeches, it is for examination.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I received a voluminous amount of documents for this witness. He was first announced as an expert for the Markale explosion, but I see now that many other elements have been produced, and I shall do my best to focus on them, leaving time, of course, for his expert report regarding the Markale shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to cover quickly some of these tabs that Mr. Groome produced. First of all, we saw a report on the possibility of manufacturing in special-purpose factories. Mr. Zecevic, this Community of the Industry of Ammunition and Military Equipment is a business association, is it not, and it has an economic nature?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not just of an economic nature. It couldn't function, as all military factories were under the direct control of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, in view of the fact that the prices of products were set by the Federal Secretariat. Therefore, they were not independent economic entities. Therefore, the Community of the Military Industry could not be an economic entity only. It was up to a part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, as you worked in a company and I worked for many years in a company, the nature of the product certainly requires a certain measure of control when we are talking about military equipment - control of the military authorities - but when talking about enterprises as such, they functioned with their own account. They had their own expenses and balance sheets, they had their own profit, they made contributions to various funds, they paid out incomes from their own earnings, they paid for their manufacturing components; therefore, they functioned on the basis of an economic account such -- like any other company in a market economy; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Every military factory in Yugoslavia constituted part of a system. It couldn't operate independently. There was the so-called principle of a common product, a joint product, which meant that within a product, the price of which was fixed by the Federal Secretariat for National Defence, every factory had a percentage share in this. This was as regards manufacturing for the needs of the Yugoslav People's Army. As for exports, not a single factory could act on its own in exports. Sales were again done by one of the institutions of the Federal Secretariat for National Defence. The distribution of funds in those factories was also controlled. So these military factories cannot be viewed as fully independent entities because they didn't decide on many things. It's rather complicated for those who don't understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, for those who don't understand the process. But as you have just explained that not a single factory produced a complete product, let me ask you, do you know how many factories took part in the production of an ordinary passenger car? Who produced the measuring instruments, the plastic parts? Who manufactured the tyres and bumpers? And it was very hard to find a factory in Yugoslavia that produced the whole -- the fixed -- the finished product on its own.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but the difference is that the prices of military products was fixed and not for Crvena Zastava products. Who fixed the prices? The market.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You worked in Pretis, didn't you? When you have a loss, when you work with a loss, who covered those losses?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We couldn't have a loss for one simple reason that Pretis always had billings up to 50 to 70 million dollars and exports accounted for 60 per cent. These were high-profit companies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So Pretis was a high-profit firm, and it acted like any other firm on the market.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: A high-profit firm but under direct control, which means that incomes, the salaries, were fixed. Personal incomes could not be increased with the increase of profits.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they never got the surpluses within Pretis?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Rarely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm surprised by that, because I think in most companies in Yugoslavia, people did receive bonuses if they worked with a profit. So this report by the Community of the Military Industry, like any kind of business association, of course this is military production, no one is denying it, but let me just read the first paragraph. "Under conditions of war in Bosnia and Herzegovina, there is still a possibility through organised cooperation with facilities in the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia to organise production in Rudi Cajavec..." which manufactured electronic components; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. They also manufactured TV sets and radio sets and all kinds of things, Rudi Cajavec, Pretis, Famos.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Famos produced engines, isn't that right, motors?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. This is a reference to special vehicles.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but engines from Famos were also used for the Priboj factory of trucks in Serbia. Then there was an association called Famos. They cooperated with Mercedes. Don't you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, you're quite right as far as automobiles are concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then Pobjeda. Pobjeda is in Gorazde, isn't it? So with other enterprises in Bosnia-Herzegovina cooperation is possible upon prior stabilisation of political circumstances, should that occur. So we have here an opinion, I would say an expert opinion of business people, and I emphasise under certain conditions, as it says, upon prior stabilisation of political circumstances should they occur. And that is all. And then there is an indication of the need for business people working in the area to focus on economic issues, and after that you were given a document on the appointment of the manager of Pretis Holding, Vogosca, and he was appointed by the government of Republika Srpska or, rather, by the Prime Minister, Professor Dr. Branko Djeric, which is also quite logical as the Republika Srpska has already been formed and Pretis was within Republika Srpska. Isn't that right, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Republika Srpska hadn't been formed then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, how come the Prime Minister, Professor Dr. Branko Djeric -- as far as I know he was Prime Minister of the Republika Srpska. He was never -- It says up there the government of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina is issuing this decision.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We can discuss this at length, but I would like to draw your attention to something else. If the president of the Community of the Military Industry of Yugoslavia is proposing the establishment of relations, why doesn't he mention the factory in Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it mentions Pobjeda, which is in Gorazde.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was thought that Pobjeda would be under the control of the Serb forces, but unfortunately, it was not possible at the time. I would like to draw your attention to the fact, could the president of an economic association such as this one, should he say the appointment with the corresponding military authorities? It is in short to coordinate security conditions and to coordinate ammunitions production, et cetera. If we're trying to say that he was just the president of an economic association, then why should he suggest that military authorities should be engaged to ensure security conditions in a factory? He should have dealt with professional matters and not military security matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: In fact, I'm going to adjourn this for a moment because the time is now up. We're going to adjourn for 20 minutes, and Mr. Zecevic, would you be, please, since you're giving evidence, to bear in mind not to speak to anybody about the evidence until it's over. Thank Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. you. Twenty minutes. We'll continue then.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will try to move on as fast as possible because we haven't got much time, Mr. Zecevic, so I'm going to ask you to give me the shortest possible answers. Of course, not to the detriment of what you're trying to say, but let's keep things within sensible proportions. So as far as I can see, a series of documents indicates that the Republika Srpska was being formed and thus regulated its own economy, including the military industrial complex. This shows this document related to the appointment of the director of Pretis Holding, where it can be seen that the government of the Serb Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina adopts this decision on the appointment of the manager of Pretis Holding and then this is signed by the Prime Minister. I assume that this is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely; it is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Along with a comment of what was going on there, Mr. Groome asked you what Pretis had to obtain from elsewhere and then you said it was electricity, coal, steam, explosives manufactured in Vitez, and that was under HVO control, then fuses in Gorazde. That was a factory that was also under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and the rest. So this was a dispersed production of elements that you spoke of. That is not in dispute either; right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is not in dispute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Further on, you were shown a longish document from the 26th of November, 1992 about the current problems of the special purposes production Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please give me the tab number so that I can follow you easily, more easily?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 5.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then what is discussed here are primarily economic and financial issues.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have to intervene at this point, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It's all right.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's not only economic issues. For example, on page 5 of this particular tab, it says that the overall claims of the special purposes factories of Republika Srpska vis-a-vis the SDPR are a certain number of dollars. $100 million. So this includes factories that at that point are under the control of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, I'm not going into the actual correctness of the information. However, the SDPR is a company that dealt with exporting the product of the specialised industry from all of Yugoslavia. Isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Precisely. But it did not have any authority at the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, but the outstanding dues remain as such; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Absolutely. But until things were legally regulated in Bosnia-Herzegovina the SDPR or anybody else, the community of the military industry, did not have the right to interfere in the internal affairs of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina which legally did exist at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All of that is well and fine, but the SDPR is not interfering in any way here. This is information about current problems of the special purposes industry of Republika Srpska and presented to the Government of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. But it seems as if nothing had changed in the sphere of influence. That's the difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I am going to tell you that they do show what was different. Towards the end of page 7, they say: "As we are geared towards them, inevitably they are in a position to blackmail us." So obviously this refers to the economic relations among different enterprises.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And they are asking for settled -- claims to be settled, for old debts to be paid. So they are talking about companies and the SDPR, about companies in the territory of Yugoslavia. They say they are a position to blackmail us, and they are asking for the payment of old debts, and in parentheses it says: "At the same time the Federal state does not wish to pay them." That is to say, the outstanding dues to our enterprises, our companies, but they are trying to put this into the general balance that will have to be struck between the federal republic of Yugoslavia and Republika Srpska and Bosnia-Herzegovina, and so on and so forth, because there has to be a division of assets. And they ask for cash advance payments for new orders. So this is a reality that is referred to in this particular document.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is exactly what is written here.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Further on, there is information about the production capacity of Pretis, and then the development of Pretis is geared in eight directions, and then it is explained that it's a special purposes and for military purposes, tool production, overhaul, machinery, dishes, then for the train car industry, transportation services, and other market-oriented programmes. This also includes some information --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Could you please give me the tab number. I simply cannot follow you, and therefore, I cannot answer your questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Tab 7 and the following.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I just quoting all of this, yes. Then, of course, the main cooperation partners, the Vitez, Duk [phoen], Nepsavic [phoen], Vlasenica, Bistrica, et cetera. All of that pertains to - how shall I put this? - the economic aspect of the manufacturing facilities of Pretis.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Military cooperation. That is a significant difference. This -- if the final product is aimed at killing people in Sarajevo, then that cannot be a very good business.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please. This is provisional information by the Pretis Holding Company to the Secretariat of the Economy of the Serb Municipality of Vogosca; isn't that right? So that's the document involved. And it explains what the capacities of Pretis are and this explanation is given to the municipality of Vogosca?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't see why anything would be in dispute in terms of this report except for the absolute substance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The substance involves the overall activity of Pretis, the one it had before the war. And it says what can be used now from among all these facilities.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Everything is fine as far as this report is concerned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Then there is the letter of the director of the holding, Mr. Milorad Motika, to -- addressed to the factory in Lucani, and then he says to them that they have provided them with casings and sets and so on, and they are asking for deliveries. This has to do with the relationship between two different companies, and it shows that, inter alia, the Lucani factory is buying something from them and selling something to them.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. According to international law, when explosives are concerned, there is a special procedure involved, and such things cannot be exported from one country to another without abiding by these rules. So this has nothing to do with business itself. They can reach an agreement, but once they agree on this, they have to abide by the regulations involved in such particular procedures. At this moment, there was a war going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina. If munitions were exported from Serbia or if parts of munitions or ordnance or fuses or cartridges were sent to Bosnia-Herzegovina, since there was an embargo, that means that that country was directly taking part in the killing of people who were unarmed. This shows the two Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. companies agreed to provide components to one another. One firm -- one of the two firms is eight kilometres away from Sarajevo, and they were supposed to manufacture munitions which were supposed to be used against the citizens of Sarajevo and Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about the things that they sell to the firm in Yugoslavia? This was there war in Yugoslavia, so what was done about that? They were selling this to the Yugoslav company?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At that point, Yugoslavia could not produce T72 and M84 components, and of course it was the objective of the Yugoslav army to have this kind of ammunition for these resources. These tanks, T72 and M84, are tanks that the Serb army in Bosnia-Herzegovina had very few of in comparison with the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much for explaining this. So the Yugoslav army was obtaining the munitions it needed from Pretis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they purchased from Pretis the things that Pretis manufactured and that Yugoslav companies could not manufacture.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: And at the same time they sold to Pretis what Pretis could not obtain in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that is the very nature of any business deal. I'll go through this very quickly because I have to move on to your expert opinion. You mentioned the Kragujevac overhaul factory. It also functions as a proper enterprise, a proper company.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. It is not a company. It has a military post code. That is a unit within the Yugoslav army. So it is not an independent economic entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But it is most certain that they collect payments for the services they render.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They collect payments.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And this is done on a commercial basis.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, generals also have their services paid for by receiving their salaries.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, this is a bit different. Please look at tab 10, I think. It says "barter deal." Precisely between the Kragujevac maintenance and repairs depot and Holding Pretis, and the two are represented by their general managers, and it is the exchange of goods between the parties that is regulated in this contract, and that is what is said -- what is provided here.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is interesting if you look at Article 2, timber and iron and Golf engines are supplied from Bosnia, and what is imported are mines, ammunitions and fuel for 120-millimetre shells. So it's barter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Everybody is buying and selling what they have or what they do not have; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There was an embargo on the import of weapons in Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There was an embargo on all of that and there were sanctions against the entire Federal Republic of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the killing of people. People were killed in Bosnia. They were killed through this barter contract in part.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As far as I know, all countries trade in weapons and military equipment, all of those who have a military industry of their own, and you know that full well since you were employed by such an industry.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: However, there are special situations when there is a crisis. Then there are special rules on the import or export of weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Groome asked you about this telex. I see that it was typed as a telegram and it refers to 125-millimetre ammunition for the M84 tank and so on and so forth. Isn't it clear that the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is buying this from Pretis?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is clear on the basis of this they are buying munitions of 125 millimetres, and they are sending to Bosnia-Herzegovina what is required to kill people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And before that, 2.000 tons of steel were sent from the Niksic steelworks.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They cannot do it because they do not have the financial resources required.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that is what is being sought; right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Again for the body of projectiles in order to kill people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, when somebody orders steel from a steel plant, then that is the production of steel --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: -- not projectile bodies.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Mr. Milosevic; there are special types of steel used for special purposes and made according to special standards with appropriate mechanical and physical and chemical characteristics that are used for projectiles. In this case the steel plant in Niksic is a specialised factory that was built for producing this special kind of steel, but it provides high-quality steel, very expensive, which is only used for manufacturing ammunition and very sophisticated parts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is true that, inter alia, the Niksic steel plant does manufacture such steel, but it is a steel plant like any other steel plant, and it makes steel. So in this tab 18, I believe, again you can see, and I just wish to make this point here, I'm not interested in the quantities at all, this is a report on issued ammunition from the Holding Pretis according to instructions issued by the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, and then the information is that in the period from the 1st of January, 1993 until the 31st of November, 1993, according to instructions issued by the Main Staff of the army of Republika Srpska, the following resources were issues from Pretis. And then there is a list several pages long showing how much was manufactured and what was sent to various units.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't refer to the manufacture. It only refers to the quantities received by the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From Pretis.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, from Pretis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So that's the difference. And then further on also, since there are many tabs, you have tab 19 where again reference is made to the fact that from Pretis for the needs of the army certain quantities of munitions are being issued; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then in tab 20, there is a survey of the munitions provided in the period between the 1st of February and the 28th of February, 1993. Then the name of each and every item, and then how much is received by individual units. You put on the ELMO the survey of Vogosca, Ilijas, Rajlovac, Sokolac, Das [as interpreted] and so on, these Pale -- these are all the different brigades that received these munitions. So what can be seen here is - how should I put this? - a continuous regular activity of the military industry of Republika Srpska, in this case Pretis, which is quite logical in a state of war; is that right, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is not being brought into question. This production could not have functioned without support from Yugoslavia. That's the problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, you see, Mr. Groome put a question to you. Certainly they received supplies from Yugoslavia. That is not being contested. The question that Mr. Groome put to you is where parts or components were imported from, and you mentioned Romania, Bulgaria, Russia. You could have mentioned all the countries of the Warsaw Pact that had similar types of weapons and from where these purchases could be made. You mentioned these countries.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I just have to correct you in one respect. This observation of mine only had to do with the 122-millimetre rocket projectiles GLAD M21 [as interpreted]. That was the specific question in terms of the markings, the cold markings on parts of projectiles that I found. They were later overhauled by the technical depot from Kragujevac.
