That is what I spoke of, because there are different ways of making these markings with different colours or by carving this in metal. That's the only reference I made. I did not mention any other munitions. 122 millimetres could not be manufactured in Pretis or in Yugoslavia because there wasn't any. It was imported. We even have photographs of this. We see the markings, and it was repaired, overhauled in Kragujevac, and then Sarajevo was targeted with these munitions. This is the whole truth. There is no dilemma, and that is what my observation referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Zecevic. Munitions or components from munitions, or components for these rocket projectiles and so on and so forth, that was purchased in the market wherever it could be purchased; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know. I was not abreast of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Since Mr. Groome asked you about some drawings, schematics and so on that had remained in Pretis and that you had the opportunity of seeing, and you say that this was designed at the Military Technical Institute. There is a single Military Technical Institute in the territory of the former Yugoslavia; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There are two. There is the air force Military Technical Institute and the ground forces technical institute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So let me correct myself. There is only one Military Technical Institute of the ground force is in the territory of the former SFRY?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was in Belgrade

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in it all systems were designed for the special purposes industry of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Until 1976. From 1976 onwards, in Bled, the military council decided that factories also had the right to be involved in R and D.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So factories had their own development sectors, and apart from them was the military engineering institute?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Therefore, these drawings, designs for rocket projectiles were made at the time when these rocket projectiles were designed, were constructed.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. These 122-millimetre rocket projectiles were never designed in the military engineering institute until 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What did these drawings that you saw refer to?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They referred to a launching ramp for rocketised bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That means that the engineers from the military institute did their professional job and manufactured certain components for launching.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but for another country.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you think they were not doing it for their own country but for another country?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: According to the information I have, that system was not introduced in the army of Serbia and Montenegro, nor has it ever been publicly displayed within a unit of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you know very well that many systems are manufactured, tested, and later either introduced or not into the system of weaponry. But in any case, the military institute had sufficient designing capacities and designers to design various things, and it was then up to the competent authorities to decide whether to introduce it or not.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The military engineering institute is a professional institution. It does not have that in its purview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I will not ask you any more about the military complex in Republika Srpska. I think this issue has been covered sufficiently here. I would like to ask you to focus on issues of your expertise regarding the Markale incident. But before I begin with specific issues, specific questions, in your statement of 1996, in paragraph 8 on page 2, you say that you volunteered to work in the investigation regarding the shelling of the Markale market; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That was on the 5th of February, 1994?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you volunteered when you heard that General Smith of the UNPROFOR said it was impossible to establish where the shell had been fired from?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And until the moment when you heard this, as you say, you were not involved in the investigation of this incident.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the moment when you heard this statement of General Smith, you were not aware of all the elements that were established or were not established by UNPROFOR teams. Isn't that obvious?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I had no access to UNPROFOR investigation teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me first one tangential thing. Do you know at what time General Smith was in Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think I was mistaken about his name anyway. It doesn't matter. Information was broadcast over the television that it was established -- it was impossible to establish where the projectile came from. I called a colleague of mine in a technical service. He invited me to come the next day. I came on site. There was a judge there. I introduced myself. I brought two of my colleagues who were ballistics experts, and the two of us were appointed competent experts who were supposed to give their report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Just let me go through the events as they went until your report. The explosion happened on the 5th of February, 1994, around noon.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it established that three UN teams came to the site of the explosion immediately after it happened?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know about that. I was in a different part of Sarajevo when it happened. Only that evening I was able to hear on the radio and television and see the footing of their reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: There were various teams, including Major Russell, Fairbud [phoen]. Did you see various documents?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I didn't see these documents until then. At the time when I joined, I was not in the army, I did not have an official position, I was simply a person who was employed in the Unis Institute, according to orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But at that time did you know that these teams had established that the shell had probably been fired from the Muslim side?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was only -- and I will acknowledge what you said about making this mistake, because General Smith was not in Bosnia at the time. Anyway, when you heard this on television, that it was impossible to establish where the shell had come from, it's only then that you volunteered.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was my duty. I'm a professional.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you reported to the security centre?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not the security centre but the criminal investigation service because I used to work with them in 1992, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you asked them for permission to get involved?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. They were not in a position to give me permission. I did not ask permission from the security centre. I addressed the judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was the judge who appointed this team of experts, including you and two of your colleagues.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And thus you and two of your colleagues received an official status.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. We were entitled to gain access to the site and make certain analyses that we thought we were able to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that's when you started your investigation which included inspection of the site, the necessary measurements, filming, et cetera. And then you reviewed television footage.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I reviewed part of the television footage when you see a soldier of the UNPROFOR retrieving the stabilising fin from the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then you made computer simulations and your own assessments, plus/minus 2, 5 per cent. You calculated the azimuth or the bearing, and you describe this on page 3 of your statement, and finally you make your expert report.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, this report, this expert finding, is dated 7 February 1994.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Correct. It took me 30 hours to complete it. If you think it can be done faster --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't think anything of the kind. I think, on the contrary, that you set out to investigate events of the 5th of February as a volunteer expressly appointed by the investigating judge and then produced a full report on the 7th of February. I find this almost impossible, because UNPROFOR experts, which I suppose are as qualified as you, had a much longer deadline to make and publish their own findings.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Will you please stop here, because you made several assertions which are not quite appropriate. First of all, UNPROFOR teams that came on site were composed of officers who were already on the territory of Sarajevo. The technical officer, an engineering officer, does not necessarily know the technology of firing. He is only trained to use weapons and ammunition, whereas my colleagues and I were professionals who have spent their entire lives designing weapons and ammunition. We had behind us years of experimental work, testing. We attended dozens of explosions of projectiles. We know Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. how munitions were produced and what they are capable of achieving. I used to teach at the mechanical engineering faculty. I was aware of the design of warheads. Don't interrupt me, it's important. The results of the technical team I was part of cannot be compared to the results and findings of the UNPROFOR experts. Also, I was aware that I had to produce a report within 24 hours. That means I had to submit it the next day, within 30 hours. And that's the difference. And if my memory serves me well, the town was under siege. It had no electricity, no water. At that particular time there was no shooting, but there was shooting the previous day when I was working. So to turn on my computer in Sarajevo, I had to use a generator to effect this computer simulation of the trajectory. Those were impossible conditions for work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Zecevic. What I'm asking you now has nothing to do with the structure of explosives or - how shall I put it? - shells or any of the things you enumerated. Can you comment on this: Captain Verdi, who arrived on site much earlier than you did, established a much greater bearing or azimuth and a much greater angle at which the shell had to make its impact without hitting the building nearby, and that's the basis on which he thought it was fired from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I make a very brief presentation, a graphic presentation of this event which will provide clear answers to these questions?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Let's just go on a bit longer. We'll look at the time, and if possible, you can do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will try to answer your question now. I had not seen that report, but I will try to explain briefly in which way I arrived at the direction from which the shell came and to assess the angle at which the shell impacted the ground. First of all, when the shell hits solid ground, activating the fuse, in the course of explosion there is a natural fragmentation of components. The splinters impact and damage the ground. In this case, we had clear scrapes of the fragments of the projectile on the ground. These scrapes are axially symmetrical. So the traces of these scrapes, the shapes of the scrapes show the direction from which the projectile arrived. On that basis, we were able to conclude that the direction was 18 degrees north north-east. That's one. Second, the projectile fell into an area between two lines of stalls, shopping stalls. The width of this corridor between stalls is on the order of about a metre. I don't have the exact figure, I can look it up later. And the height of the stalls is about two metres. And if we use simple geometric arithmetic that we know from primary school - you don't need high education - you can realise that the minimal impact degree is 55 degrees. That is the lower -- lowest estimate, because if the angle had been lower, the projectile would have hit the roof of the stall. If we approach directly the place of the -- the spot of the explosion and if we look at the recording, the video, we see an opening in the ground where the stabiliser fin was sticking from. I asked for the stabiliser fin to be brought, and without any effort I put it back in the ground to the depth of 250 millimetres. I used a quadrant, which is an instrument for measuring elevation, and I measured the angle of inclination of this stabiliser fin. It was about 60 degrees. Since this stabiliser fin had been retrieved from the ground before, I thought as a professional that it would be unprofessional of me to determine the angle at exactly 60 degrees. I took a margin of error of plus/minus 5 per cent, and I thought it was fair to admit I could have made a small margin of error. Those are purely technical discussions. Based on these findings, I determined that the angle of impact was around 60 degrees, the direction was from -- of the trajectory was 18 degrees north north-east, and I took into account the structure of scrapes on the ground. On that basis, I saw that the traces on the ground were not axially symmetrical, which shows that the projectile hit the ground at a certain angle. As I said, around 60 degrees. The very finding that when the projectile hit the ground, after the explosion the stabiliser fin was stuck into the ground means that the projectile had a very high velocity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Sorry. I have to finish. On that basis, it was very easy to determine the location at six possible points. If you take into account that the stabiliser fin is stuck into the ground, that is only possible at velocities higher than 100 metres/second. And based on ballistic analysis, it could have been at velocities of 4.900, 5.000 or 6.600 metres/second. So the nearest distance between VRS and the Muslim side was 1.900 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it in dispute that Major Russell determined that the projectile fell at a degree of 67 to 73 degrees?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't see his report, so I can't say whether it was in dispute or not. Second, I don't know on what basis he determined that. All that I presented in my then report and in my subsequent reports used during the trial of General Galic is clear as to what basis it is founded on. You can only tell me on what the findings of the major are based.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In any case, Mr. Zecevic, it seems logical that you should look at the reports of other teams and the team of the UNPROFOR who made all the other measurements in addition to making your report, because you must admit that you have a conflict of interest. You immediately volunteered to be one of the investigators in this incident with a prejudice that it must have been fired by Serbs, whereas the UN had several teams whose findings differ from yours. How do you explain this discrepancy?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I volunteered because 68 of my co-citizens were killed and 274 were wounded. My children, my sister, my brother and their children could have been among them. My friends were there. And that is why I volunteered to establish that. I didn't volunteer to give any publicity to myself. Let me finish, please. There's something else I wish to say. Why would I look at reports of any of the UN officers if that report was never shown to me? Secondly, my position in Sarajevo was not such for me to be given a report or someone to call me to read the report. If the Prosecutor asked me to provide an additional report, they never felt it necessary to give me those reports, so I'm saying that I didn't have a chance to look at them. Thirdly, I think that it is better as an independent author without looking at what others had written to write my own report. And whoever reads it will find that there's absolutely not a single error in it in terms of the physical description of the event. There are no fabrications nor any subjective opinions but very exact and precise facts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Doesn't your subjective opinion -- isn't it reflected in the text of the report when the army of Republika Srpska is referred to as Chetnik forces, aggressor forces, et cetera? And yet you're an expert who is called upon to establish professionally the trajectory of the shell.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, TV Pale took pride in calling themselves Chetniks, and I was just repeating that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If they thought that, you will agree that you didn't believe that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I was a patriot who loved Yugoslavia during Tito's era, let me tell you. And I couldn't believe that there could be a trained armed unit that could be capable of killing women and children in a Sarajevo under siege.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is not in dispute that that was tragic. We are talking here about your expert report regarding a shell.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But Chetniks have nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But then there are reports of other teams. And my question was why you didn't compare their results, and you said that was not necessary.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I didn't have access. That's the point. I didn't know about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll go on to very concrete questions and please give me brief answers because you are spending a lot of time, and I have been very patiently listening to you. The area of the Markale market, was it in the same condition as it was immediately after the explosion, when you went there?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, for one reason, because 24 hours had gone by. Sixty-eight people had been killed. There was a lot of blood, and the area had been cleaned.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the area had been cleaned, and only then did you start your investigation. Do you believe as an expert that the main conditions for a reliable finding did not exist because the area had been cleaned before you started your expert investigation?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At the time, it had no substantive impact on the nature of my report. It could affect the number of people killed, where they were killed, et cetera, but the actual point of impact, no. If you go to Sarajevo, you can have a look. You can see the imprints of fragments and shells all over Sarajevo. In Markale, certainly not, because it's been reconstructed?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I must say unfortunately so. I don't know who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In addition to UNPROFOR, the police authorities in Sarajevo carried out an investigation and took away the elements found, fragments and pieces. So the area was cleaned, the pieces taken away, and then you and your team start your investigation.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't need any fragments. I only needed the stabiliser. The opening that this stabiliser was lodged into was quite undamaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the basis for your expert opinion regarding this whole event was the stabiliser which had been taken away and then given to you.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: One of the bases. Not the only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, what was the basis for your expert report if it was not just the stabiliser?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I explained at the beginning. If necessary, I shall repeat myself but that will take a lot of time. I told you. The angle of descent is the basis, the appearance, et cetera, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see. You've already explained that, so there's no need to repeat it. And what was the condition of the actual point of explosion when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, as pieces had been taken out, the area cleaned, what was the condition of the place? It wasn't dug over. Of course it was when you can see on the video that knives were used to pick out the pieces and fragments of the mine, of the shell.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I apologise. Digging in our language implies the use of a pickaxe or a spade. But this is a fine tool, a knife that was used to delicately pick out the stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what was the damage on the ground, on the spot?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can show you the photographs. I have them here for you to see if you wish. I can't describe them to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, in your earlier testimony at General Galic's trial, you said that on the spot you only found two pieces of the explosive device, and that the stabiliser was given to you by the police which you, after your study, returned to the police; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on the spot of the explosion, apart from damage on the ground, you didn't have any material evidence of the explosive device on the spot of the explosion itself when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Except for the video shots of the moment when the stabiliser was taken out and the whole process, but that is quite unimportant for my subsequent analyses.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You wrote, on page 25505, that on the basis of the video recording you said that, "The frontal surface of the stabiliser in our assessment had an angle of 20 to 30 in relation to the surface of the ground," and then there's picture 3 in brackets. So tell me, please --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You wrote that on the basis of the video recording.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Let me find it, please. Having insight into the video recording made immediately after the explosion, it can be noted -- it can be noted that the stabiliser of the projectile penetrated 20 to -- 200 to 250 millimetres into the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I have a quotation here that, "The stabiliser formed an angle of 20 to 30 degrees in relation to the surface of the ground (figure 3)." Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I see. The frontal surface, yes. And then by reconstructing the position of the stabiliser, the angle of its frontal surface in relation to the ground was about 30 degrees, and in relation to the mortar shell about 60 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, how is it possible on the basis of a picture given to you by the police, without knowing the angle of filming and the position of the camera, how can you determine the angle between the stabiliser fin and the ground?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: If you don't see the photograph, it's difficult for me to explain. I am a technical expert, and angles for me are quite normal. I can easily assess whether it's 20 or 30 degrees. It is easy to establish that. That was what I was trained to do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I suggest, Dr. Zecevic does have a very clear photograph of the scene as he saw it. It may be of assistance to the Chamber if it's placed on his ELMO. He has it in his possession.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, let's do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And since it's mentioned, I think the Chamber also needs the original copy of the pictures which appear in his report. It's very difficult to follow in this circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I'll get better pictures.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Just a moment. We're just going to look at the photograph.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I placed the stabiliser into this opening - there's a difference of quality in the image - there's no major difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you make those photographs? Who took these photographs?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't make any of these, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Were they taken by the Sarajevo police?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Sarajevo police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I think this is a very important fact. You say, "Having insight into the video recording made immediately after the explosion, it can be noted that the stabiliser of the projectile entered the ground to a depth of 200 to 250 millimetres." That's what you wrote, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So on this basis you were not able to exactly measure the depth of the opening.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I didn't determine the depth on the basis of the photograph. I just said that when I reconstructed the event and placed the stabiliser into the opening, I was able to measure exactly the depth as we know what the length of the stabiliser fin is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you say 200 to 250 millimetres.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Logically so. That can be seen from this first photograph. You can see the front of the stabiliser is almost on a level with the asphalt. And in view of the length of the stabiliser being about 200 millimetres, then that is it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you can see on both photographs that the angle is large, because the shell fell almost vertically.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When I said an angle of 20 degrees, it's an angle between the front of this stabiliser. The front. This front. And when you apply it to the axis, that is 90 minus 20, which makes it 70 degrees, or 90 minus 30, making it 60. So technically you didn't read my report carefully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I did read your report very carefully, but you should know that, for instance, Captain Verdi at 1500 hours on the 5th of February - which means before you - determined that the minimum angle at which the mine -- the shell could have flown over the nearby building is about 80 degrees in relation to the surface of the ground at the marketplace. Major Russell, on the same day at 1630 hours, measured 1.200 to 1.300 degrees, that is, the angle was 48 to 73 degrees. So 80, 73 degrees, and the pitch itself that you have shown when you reconstructed it, that the shell fell almost vertically, which is an indication that it was fired from the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, can I show you some new photographs to respond to this question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the site of the event, and that is why I consider it to be very important. These stories that a mortar shell should have hit a building are ridiculous for one simple reason: The point of impact of the projectile was 4.16 metres from the closest building, which is not higher than six metres, and the right hand building, this building, this is this building, this is the angle of descent, is 11.1 metres away. If we proceed from the fact that the projectile arrived at an angle of 45 degrees, which is absurd, then the height of the building would need to be about 11 metres, and that building has three or four stories. And in view that the angle of descent was about 60 degrees, this is this angle, then there's no chance that the projectile could have hit the building. And if you have forgotten, I said that the projectile fell into a space between two stalls. This is an absolutely narrow, limited area about one metre wide. So that is an angle of -- a minimum angle of 55 degrees. So that is why I said 60 degrees plus/minus 5 degrees. So there's no question of a mortar shell hitting a building. The main purpose of mortar shells is for them to act -- to be used behind obstacles, behind buildings. They have a broad spectrum of action. It was clearly shown that the -- that the angle of impact was 60 degrees. There's no discussion over that. The fact that a major or captain said something else, he doesn't tell us how he obtained that angle. My report states clearly how I calculated that angle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, is that picture or drawing included in your expert report?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is in a somewhat different form. It's the same picture, actually. These are very important -- this is a very important photograph I would like to say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If you could tell -- if you could tell us what are the same pictures as that. Picture 1 and picture 3?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is a picture showing the area immediately surrounding the point of impact.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We have difficulty, because the picture does not appear in the English translation. I've got it, thanks to the registrar. Yes, please go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [no translation].

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that the tail fins -- between the tail fins and the ground is 20 to 30 degrees, and then on the same page you say that the angle is about 60 degrees, and you consider it more reliable than those measured by UNPROFOR officials immediately after the explosion.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I'm talking about the angle of the front surface. If we consider this to be the body of the stabiliser, I said -- and this was dug into the ground. So I could only measure this angle. And let me say that the angle is 20 to 30 degrees. Whereas this other angle is 90 minus this one. This is simple mathematics. This is something you learn in secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Surely you're not going to tell us, Mr. Zecevic, that these UN experts did not have absolutely any qualifications to carry out any measurements and investigations. I assume that the UN also sent trained officers who are able to establish what happened. The point of impact of a shell is no great science.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I have no idea who the UN sent, nor am I interested in that. I am just commenting on the report -- nor should I comment on UN reports. I can only comment on my own report. Please don't attribute to me something that I didn't say. I'm just not interested in that. If I need to explain something from my own report, I will do so, but I didn't see those reports, nor can I comment on them. And I don't want to comment on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, then don't. I see that you're all worked up.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm quite calm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't look that way. But I'm not going to ask you whether you read the report. But in the UNPROFOR report, on the 5th of February, 1994, paragraph 6, it says there are reasons to believe that at that time, the authorities dug through the crater in detail. Is that your opinion too or do you think they did not?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So they did not dig through the crater?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It was not dug. What does it mean in detail or superficially? I told you what it means to dig. I showed you here the actual place where this happened, what I found on site. I put the stabiliser here. And if you look at the damage, the damage shows that the mortar projectile was at an angle between 55 or 65 degrees when it originally fell. And vertically it was close to 90 degrees. Had it been vertical, then the damage would have been on various sides. However, most of the asphalt damage is in the area where the mortar shell came from, and that corroborates what the expertise said.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On page 002531, you -- "However, the fact that there are no colours on the stabiliser shows that this was probably recent war production." I'm going to omit some parts. Never mind. "And this indicates that it was probably manufactured in one of the two factories that made this kind of thing before, Marko Oreskovic, Licki Osik, or Vogosca." Is that right? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please try to answer my questions now without going into lengthy speeches. Do you know that UNPROFOR officers, when they toured the 105th Brigade of the 1st Corps - that is the 1st Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, is that right - on the 9th of February, 1994, at the ammunition depot saw 120-millimetre mines that had not been coloured, and they saw the same ones -- this is page 0303831, and this is an UNPROFOR report of the 15th of February, 1994. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. There's no reason for me to know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Such shells that you claim were made in Vogosca or Licki Osik were seen by UNPROFOR controllers on the positions of the 105th Brigade of the Sarajevo Corps.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know. I could not discuss the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If you don't know that, I'm just indicating it to you. But this part of your report is under a question mark then, because this is absolutely the same thing that they saw in your case.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: At this moment it does not affect the conclusions of this report at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Can we move a bit faster then. What's the altitude of the Markale market?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: About 550 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: About 600 metres? According to the information I have, it's about 600 metres. On the basis of which estimate did you conclude --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down; the interpreters cannot follow at this pace. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of which estimate did you assess that 400 metres is the distance between the point of impact and the point of firing?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. This is the area above Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The point of impact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We're not talking about the altitude of the Markale market. It is 600 metres.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I've already said to you that we looked at 200 metres and 400 metres, and we worked with 400 metres because, of the six possible places from which this projectile could have been fired, five were at an altitude close to 400 metres above the Markale market.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Do you know that in this trajectory of 18 degrees north-east plus/minus 5, as you established this, the highest altitudes and elevations are up to 1.086 metres? That is 23496 or, or rather, in the Serbian language, page 02115548. So if what you are claiming were correct, somebody would have to put this mortar on the top elevations in order to have this 400 metre difference, which had to be there.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It did not have to be there. You misunderstand this difference. This 400 or 200 or 300 or 500 metre difference is only a very small segment in terms of determining the actual point more precisely. It could have been 00. It has nothing to do with it. I did not know from which position this projectile was fired. I only knew the direction, the trajectory. And in order to carry out a ballistic analysis, it was necessary for me to be able to estimate the point where it was potentially launched in order to take into account the correction factors in terms of the altitude between the point where it was launched and the point where it impacted. It doesn't matter. Both of us can say that there is a difference between the point of impact and all the five possible places from which the projectile could have been launched. I tell you once again, there are six possible points for a mortar. Five points are directly under the control of the army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, don't you know that a 120-millimetre mortar, as you know better than I do, is a bulky weapon? It is not put on the very top of an elevation but at someplace to which one has access. And in this direction that you are describing, there was no possibility for the army of Republika Srpska to place a mortar at such a high altitude as you had established.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Physically this is impossible.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Somebody gave you the wrong kind of information, Mr. Milosevic. There is no summit. There is no elevation. It is not mentioned at all. It could have been a meadow. These are hillocks there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Oh, so you don't even know the distance. You cannot even determine the distance from which it was fired. The only important thing is that it came from Serb positions, then it had to be there. Six, five, four, you can just go on guessing.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you need three square metres in order to position a mortar. If you're trying to put it on top of a building, then people are going to do that if they deem it necessary. But if you tell me that a 120-millimetre mortar cannot be put at any such point, then the advisors who are giving you advice are not giving you the best type of counsel, are not the best possible counsellors.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, is it of any significance to you that the military observers of the UN reported that there was no report concerning the opening of fire from the Kosevska Brigade on the 5th of February, 1994? "The explosion in the market was registered by military observers on the Bosnian side as incoming fire but the point where it came from was not registered." I quoted the UN report to you directly now.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the UN observers register the firing of audio systems. So they either hear it through an audio system or with their very own ears. As sound moves through space, it involves a very complex process. Now, it depends on whether there are buildings, whether there are forests, whether there is fog, whether there is humidity. So you can place a mortar in a valley surrounded by woods. So people who are four kilometres away will not be able to feel the difference in terms of the firing of such a projectile. Or if you put it out in an open clearing, then there is going to be an amazing difference in the noise levels. So this is not in contrast with my report. The projectile came from the direction that was 18 degrees north or north-east. I showed that it had to have sufficient energy, at least at the impact moment, of 200 metres/second so that the stabiliser could be placed this way. That is the key point, and that is how these first three points are eliminated from where the firing could have taken place. So it is possible, because the stabiliser was sticking into the ground, that is sufficient proof that the projectile had to have a greater velocity of impact and that it had been launched from the -- with the fourth, fifth, or sixth charge, and that is a distance of 4.900, 5.000 something, and 6.400 metres. No one can establish through any kind of expertise from which of these three points it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But why did you change the attitude [as interpreted] in respect of the Markale altitude?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, look. Above the market are hills. So 30 metres above the market there is a hill. Whoever looked at this place could see that. I can show it to you here. This is it. This is it. In relation to this, I looked at 200 metres to 400 metres. I can also make an analysis with 200 metres that will show you that the distance is not 4.900 metres but 4.800 metres. It doesn't mean a thing in terms of its precise determination.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is important that we should get answers, your answers in this respect, because of course I'm going to challenge this, given adequate expert support. And also tell me, if a mine stabiliser of 120 millimetres has a fin and is to fall into ground, asphalt, and you give the figure of 200 to 250 millimetres in your report, there was asphalt there and then underneath there was sand --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please don't simplify matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What should be the velocity of impact of that mine so that it would remain the way you had put it?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I told you that the minimum had to be 200 metres/second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what is the average radius of operation of such a mine?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: According to available data, about 17 metres. That would be the radius.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, what is more precise when the angles are smaller when a mine is fired, as you say in paragraph 3 of your previous report? It says that if the mortar crew has the possibility of choosing the angle -- my question is actually does this angle imply greater precision?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: 45 -- 40 degrees and above.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: 40 degrees and above.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That means when they are on the same plane, the objective and the point from where the mine is fired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: The time has come to take the adjournment. Mr. Milosevic, we will have to finish this at quarter to 2:00 in order to finish with this witness. Perhaps, if you look at Mr. Tapuskovic's position, if you can provide some time for him, I'm sure he'd be grateful. Yes. We'll adjourn now. Twenty minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please take into account the time needed for Mr. Tapuskovic. I will leave that much time for him so that we are able to finish within this session.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, what is the probability for one shell, one 120-millimetre shell to hit a target of --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speaker please slow down. Could we have the question repeated.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Sorry to interrupt you, but Mr. Milosevic, could you repeat the question again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked what is the probability of one 120-millimetre shell hitting a pre-planned target sized 23 by 28 metres at a distance of 2.000 metres from the artillery position?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell you without looking at the firing table, because I have to point out certain dilemmas you have to face. If you are trying to hit a target for the first time, and if you are just positioning the mortar on the position for the first time, then the probability is lower. It is less likely that you will hit the target. But if you have several attempts and if you had the benefit of previously making adjustments as was the case here because the war had been going on for some time, people were familiar with their weapons, there are so-called standard and accidental mistakes. Standard mistakes, standard errors are typical of certain weapons, where accidental, occasional mistakes are due to the weather, et cetera. So if you take occasional mistakes, you have to take into account whether the position is familiar to you, whether you are targeting a target that is familiar to you, that you tried to hit before regardless of whether it is Markale or some other target. In any case, I cannot give you a precise answer without consulting the firing tables.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Artillery officers and UNPROFOR officers claimed that the probability of hitting the Markale market with one shell without adjusting fire is very small when firing from a great distance. Do you agree that the probability of hitting the target is much higher from a smaller distance?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Don't you think it was the case indeed that the market was hit from a smaller distance?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It has nothing to do with it, Mr. Milosevic. You are forgetting certain physical factors. We cannot change the nature, we can only try to understand it. Nature is very clear here. The shell exploded. The angle of impact is around 60 degrees. The stabiliser fin was buried in the ground. It couldn't have been buried in the ground 200, 250 millimetres unless the velocity of the impact was more than 200 metres/second. Mr. Milosevic, I heard you out. Please hear me out too. You asked me a question, and give me time to answer. I'm telling you again, you cannot introduce arguments into science without any basis in fact. These are exact facts that are not subject to discussion. We have exact facts that point to the origin of fire. Mortars are among the most precise artillery weapons. Both you and I know that the most dangerous weapon in the Second World War for the partisan forces were mortars. In the war in Sarajevo and in Bosnia-Herzegovina, most victims were killed by mortars.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, what is the possible error, in metres, regarding the target?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I am telling you again, Mr. Milosevic: Without knowing the parameters, what kind of crew we have, what the corrections are, et cetera, I cannot answer you. You can look up the textbook on the theory of firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Answer one question for me regarding outside observations. Is it possible from a distance of over 2.000 metres, based on the possible sound, can you determine the point of origin of a shell? And you -- if you as an expert cannot determine it, can a simple ordinary citizen do that who doesn't have any familiarity with mortars?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the problem of spread of sound is very well studied.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about the spread of sound. Is it possible to determine the origin of fire if something was fired from a distance of 2.000 metres?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Look, modern systems for determining the origin of fire were -- are based on sound, audio equipment. You need three localisers of sound in order to determine the origin of fire. These are well-known systems in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked this because we had here a citizen, a witness who claimed that he had heard a mortar shell being fired. Thank you very much for providing this explanation about the three localisers of sound. Now, tell me, how many shells need to be fired in order to make an adjustment to the target?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I think you're talking to the wrong man if you want an answer to this. I am not operating or running a battery of mortars to be able to answer this. Without consulting firing tables or textbooks, I cannot give you a precise answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That is enough. Regarding the video where we see an UNPROFOR soldier digging out the stabiliser fin, do you agree that it is clear in this video that at the moment when the UNPROFOR soldier is beginning to work the stabiliser is not visible? We can only see it after the soldier has removed a layer of what looks like debris, using a knife.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can't tell you now. You must have seen this video. It was a long time since I saw it, maybe ten years.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What was the composition of the ground on the market?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: There was a layer of asphalt 1.5 to 2 centimetres thick, sand and earth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. If the shell detonated upon impacting the ground upon asphalt, in what direction does the impact wave act, in depth or in width?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, may I show you this picture? It is an x-ray of a detonation of a projectile very similar to the one we're talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it the same one?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It doesn't matter. The physical process is the same. This is a 122-millimetre projectile, so the calibre is very similar. The picture is not upside down. It is sitting on the ELMO very well. You don't have to read the text, it doesn't matter. This is the moment when the projectile is hitting an obstacle or when the fuse is activated, and this white spot you see is the beginning, the activation of the detonation wave, and then a reaction and burst begin. And on the following picture you can see that the projectile is growing wider. It is now almost double the size. And the flow of the products of detonation has begun towards the ground. The flow is at a velocity of 10.000 millimetres/second. It is those products of detonation that create the damage.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: My question was: What is the direction of the impact wave, in the width or in the depth?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: When the projectile bursts, the impact wave is directed on all sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: From the detonation of the fuse, is the detonation, the impact, determined by --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't hear the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You cannot see this on the picture. When the detonation happens, fragments start moving through space.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So both up and laterally?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, on all sides. All over the place. There are various estimates, depending on the velocity of impact. Various deviations in the distribution of fragments are possible, and we can arrive at certain values. I'm showing you this example. Let us take this case. When the greatest number of fragments are in this lateral part, the lowest speed of fragments are in these two parts, and the lowest mass is also in these two parts, although on the side you can still find a significant number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: This impact wave rejects fragments all over; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's not what I said. I said the products of detonation during explosion destroy the structure of the body of the projectile. Cracks appear. And as a result of pressure inside, which is 250 to 300.000 bars, and a very high temperature of about 3.000 degrees Celsius, these detonations accelerate metallic fragments and they can move about 1.500 to 2.000 metres/second depending on their mass.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Is it possible for this material that is propelled by explosion to be found again on the spot where it was propelled?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: From which part of the projectile?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Any part. The projectile hit the ground, exploded, propels material all over. As you said, is it possible for this propelled material to be found again on the spot?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Some parts can be found here, for instance fragments of the fuse. And these scrapes, if you had occasion to see them on the asphalt, they were propelled. They hit the asphalt. They had no energy to bounce further, and they fell again on the asphalt or perhaps they hit somebody who was nearby.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Tell me, is it then probable, precisely according to this video where you see the stabiliser covered by pebbles and earth, and it is not actually visible, doesn't it prove that the stabiliser fin did not lodge in the ground? It was put there.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The process described is on the order of the 30 millionth part of a second. There is no stabilisation there involved. Why don't you start from the premise that after detonation, when this cylindric part of the projectile fell apart, this part of the stabiliser continued to travel through space and entered this area and penetrated 250 millimetres into the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wasn't it propelled?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, it couldn't have been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It wasn't propelled? You're saying that it was buried? How come it wasn't propelled by explosion?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Because the process of detonation was on the order of 170 plus/minus 20 metres/second. If the velocity was minimally 200 metres/second, in order for the stabiliser to lodge it should have a residual kinetic energy of, let's say, 40 to 60 metres per second and then it gets buried. In such cases, depending on velocity of the projectile at the time of impact, we can have three possibilities. When it is launched with the first, second, or third charge, or let's say just first and second charge, then the speed of fall is lower than the speed of propelling, and then it goes back in the direction from which it was fired. However, if the speed of impact is around 170, 160, 150 metres/second, we will find the stabiliser fin lying somewhere in the vicinity. If the speed of impact is 200 or more metres/second, then the stabiliser fin will get buried in the ground. So these are three possibilities. Operating with these three possibilities, we can decide from which possible area it was fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Some ballistics experts, and I saw some among UN experts, claim that it should been propelled, rejected. It wouldn't have been buried under pebbles and sand. It must have been put there later.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the experts I knew at the military engineering institute with whom I worked for 17 years had occasion together with me to determine -- to determine whether stabilisers were involved in such cases or not. There is no dilemma here, whatever some experts may say. In my follow-up report, you have findings of an American laboratory for ballistical analysis which give you precise data for determining the velocity of this stabiliser.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It was not rejected or propelled. It was buried, as we saw in that video.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I didn't say that. You also have the velocity of descent of at least 100 metres/second. If you take into account that speed of descent, you have the residual kinetical energy with which it lodged into the ground. I'll repeat this to make it clearer. When the velocity is smaller than the speed of impact, then the projectile lodges into the ground. When the speed of descent is equal to the speed of impact, the stabiliser is found in the area. When the speed of descent is higher, then it will be buried in the ground. For instance, with 60 or 82-millimetre shells, you will almost never find them buried in the ground because the speed of descent, the speed of firing, is lower than the speed of impact on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can we now conclude that your expert report, as it is, and I don't agree with it, did not remove a reasonable doubt that the shell was fired onto Markale by Serbs, because you found also one possible origin of fire in the Muslim territory as well. So that reasonable doubt was not removed even by the findings of other experts?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In my report, it says explicitly that there are six possible origins of fire for this mortar projectile that correspond to the conditions of impact that we are faced with. But as I said earlier, for the stabiliser to be lodged in the ground, it had to have a velocity higher than 200 metres/second. That inevitably means that the projectile was launched with fourth, fifth, or sixth trajectories higher than 4.900 metres. That means more elevated positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the higher velocity of firing, the greater the distance.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. The angle of impact, the velocity of penetration of these stabilisers are the parameters which point out to three possible origins of fire; at 4.900 metres, around 5.000, and 6.300 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Your conclusions are clear, but let us look at this diagram. Is it possible for the projectile to have been fired from this vehicle?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Will you place it on the ELMO, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What are you telling me with this vehicle? What has it got to do with this firing of the shell?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not clear to me. It's quite unimportant whether it came from a vehicle or a mortar. The question is where the mortar was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's precisely it. The mortar could be on this vehicle, and forces of the BH army had such a vehicle which they used to fire shells, and it is possible that it was fired from this vehicle.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'd rather not go into that discussion. My study clearly showed that the direction was 18 degrees north north-east, six possible firing positions. Later on, I indicated three firing position, fourth, fifth, and sixth charge. If this vehicle could have been 4.900 metres away in territory held by the army of Republika Srpska, then it's possible, if they wanted to let this vehicle be placed in that position, but I won't go into that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that is what I'm claiming, and this coincides with the findings of the UN experts, that it is possible that the shell was fired from territory controlled by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The farthest position held by the BH army was 1.900 metres away. And I am telling you all three locations from which these effects could have been produced is 4.900, 5.400, and 6.400 metres away.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But I have another sketch here which shows the original damage on the asphalt and the subsequent made, handmade, damage on the asphalt, which are indicated by dotted line and the original ones in a straight line. And this is what could be deduced from UN experts' reports. Would you like to comment on these, please? In your opinion, is it possible that these two directions, called confusions because of subsequent damage that was hammered into the ground --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, this is a sketch made by hand and not a photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Of course it is a sketch. How can you on a photograph indicate an arrow?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: But what you're talking about, mechanical intervention on the site of the explosion? Here is the site of the explosion. Now, give me a photograph like this - you have the video recording in the presence of the UN officer - and tell me whether there's any difference. Now, a drawing made like this could be that of an artist. As you see, the dotted line indicates the damage hammered in subsequently -- you're showing us a sketch. There is no subsequent intervention on these photographs. I'd like your experts to come to Sarajevo. No one will stop them nowadays. They can have a look at the point of impact and see whether there is any additional intervention done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But as you said yourself, the Markale marketplace has been completely reconstructed.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but there are other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But the traces have been destroyed once and for all now. But you said generally that an elementary school is sufficient to understand this, and I assume that the UN officers who made these reports had at least elementary training.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you again I never saw a single UN officer report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I should just like to draw your attention to one further point. You testified in the Galic case as well, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And in this document that has to do with General Galic, entitled "Judgement and Opinion," in Chapter 7, separate and dissenting opinion --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I can't follow because I don't have the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The dissenting opinion of Judge Nieto-Navia --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm not necessarily going to stop you saying what the objection or any other other form of judgement may have been, but it's not necessary -- it may or not be the case that it's necessary for a witness to know anything about this. So he may well not be able to answer it, but you can and you can put something provided you put it very briefly and it's relevant.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. May, this dissenting opinion consists of many pages and I will read out only a few lines from it, so I will be extremely brief. Don't worry, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So point 97. It says: "[In English] For the above reasons, I am not satisfied that the Prosecution has established beyond a reasonable doubt that the SRK fired the shell which exploded in Markale market on 5th February, 1994. I do not reach this conclusion idly because the ABH as well as SRK had access during the conflict to 120-millimetre mortars which are weapons which can be transported with relative ease. Finally, I know that my conclusion about the origin of fire also finds support in the special UN team's official finding communicated to the UN Security Council that there --" [Interpretation] then a quotation -- "[In English] is not sufficient physical evidence to prove that one party or the other fired the mortar bomb." [Interpretation] That is all I wanted to quote from this dissenting opinion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. I haven't stopped you doing it, but normally, of course, that is a view. It's a matter which we have to take into account and it's not a matter for comment. Now, if you'd like to go on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, Mr. May. I will continue with my questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, is it true that it was only six days later on the 11th of February that an investigation was started by the so-called special UN team consisting of Captain Jose Grande, Commander John Hamill, and Major Sajis Arkan [phoen]? Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I don't see how I could remember. I have repeatedly said that I haven't seen a single report of the United Nations regarding this incident. I did not take part in their work. I did my work and completed it in two days' time during the war on the 6th and 7th, and since then I was not consulted up until 1995 when there was an explosion in TV Sarajevo building. And throughout that intervening period, no one contacted me, so I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you then. Four days after they conducted an investigation, they produced a report, and I'm asking you how do you explain that this special UN team needed four days to compile their report whereas you, in such a short time, having heard on television that the point of firing cannot be established, you were appointed, completed your study, and had a report ready already on the 7th. Are they that much less capable than you or perhaps are there any other reasons to explain this?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you read my report and what I wrote in it together with my colleagues, and it was completed in two days, we just estimated or indicated six possible locations, and we said that only one of them was in the territory held by the BH army. My subsequent studies over the past two years, at the request of the Prosecution, I carried out more detailed analyses, and on the basis of what I have repeatedly said today, I showed that out of those six locations the fourth, fifth, and sixth are those that fulfil the necessary requirements. I had an order from the investigating judge that I had to complete my report within 24 hours, and in accordance with that order, because he was the person who appointed me, I completed my work in a professional manner within the time available and the facts given. Through subsequent analyses, the results of which I have given to the Prosecution, produced what I have testified about today. Therefore, I am not calling in question at all the ability of UN officers. You have your own opinion. I have my own technical opinion. It is up to Their Honours, the Judges, to assess which documents they will rely on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: If on the 15th of February they stated that it was impossible to establish who fired the shell --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That is their right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But their first reports, initial reports indicate that it had been done by the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I have no idea, Mr. Milosevic. I haven't read those reports. I can only talk about what I did. I'm no official person in Bosnia-Herzegovina. I'm an ordinary citizen, a university professor, and that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And is it true that your engagement has nothing to do with the statement of the UNPROFOR representative to the effect that it cannot be established because they produced their final report on the 15th?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Surely there's no need for me to repeat what I said in my statement. I heard on television and the radio that they had stated that it cannot be established, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. In your statement in 1996, in paragraphs four and five, I quote: "As a member of the team of experts at the beginning of the war, I organised in Sarajevo the production of weapons, the production and development of weapons." I will slow down for the interpreters. You said: "As a member of a team of experts at the beginning the war, I organised in Sarajevo the production and development of weapons. We worked in cooperation with the staff of the BH army. I worked there until the 14th of December, 1993, when the team was disbanded." Is that right, Mr. Zecevic?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: That's right. I was replaced.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you stopped working in that area one month and 20 days prior to the explosion at Markale?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. I was replaced in July 1993 when the head of the staff of the BH army, General Sefer Halilovic, was replaced. Then the entire unit of which I was a member was also dismissed. For six months, I was at their disposal. They didn't know what to do with me. And then on the 14th of December, they gave me the order to go to the UNIS Institute. I was under military obligation, and I went there. Therefore, my engagement as head of the department for research and development attached to the Main Staff of the BH army lasted from June 1992 until July 1993. When my unit was dismissed and disbanded I was put on hold, and I was at their disposal. They didn't know what to do with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your CV, on page -- it says that from 1st of June until the 18th of December, 1993, you were employed in the General Staff of the BH army and the mechanical engineering faculty in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In the centre for special purpose industry, the department for research and development, attached to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The Main Staff of the ABiH army?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But that is the General Staff of the army.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. It's a unit attached to the staff. I was not a member of the General Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that you were a member of the General Staff, but you were employed by them.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: All soldiers are, in a sense, employed by the General Staff. So please don't attribute what you're saying to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not doing that, I am just quoting what you said, that you were employed in the General Staff of the ABiH army as head of the department for research and development.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. In the centre for special purpose production and research department, working attached, not in the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Okay, attached to the Main Staff. And you worked on the design of projectiles.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Under conditions when there were no manufacturing components and spare parts, I had to find ways of the BH army ensuring for itself within Sarajevo the process of production of munitions, and this engagement lasted one year.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 37 in your statement of July 2002, you described how you used unexploded shells that you collected in the territory of Sarajevo to make appropriate lethal devices.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because 60 per cent of our needs for explosives were solved in that way. Every kilogramme of explosive in an unexploded shell would be worth one bomb, and so people, at the risk of their lives, found these unexploded ordnances, I had the explosives extracted for it to be reprocessed for defence purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So I did perhaps -- one of the possible findings of the investigation could have been that a device exploded in Markale that you yourself may have participated in making.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: In Pretis, yes, but before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And not out of what you described that you made out of unexploded devices.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: We made hand grenades and rifle grenades for personal defence, not those that could be used by larger units. We were unable to produce 120-millimetre mortar shell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is it quite clear that you have a direct interest in not establishing that the BH army fired the shell?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't wish to comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But you were working for the staff of that army.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I was working for the defence of the citizens of Sarajevo, my friends and relatives. The unit I was in command of, 30 per cent were Serbs, 21 per cent were Croats, the rest were Bosniaks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could there be pauses, please. It is impossible to follow at this speed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You're making it very hard for the interpreters, for everybody. So would you both make a pause. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I did not ask about other members of your unit. I was saying isn't it clear that it was more than evident that you had an interest involved in order not to have it established that it was the BH army who fired at Markale?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I worked in a professional manner. In my report there is not a single thing that is partial in any way. You can send this report to my colleagues from the Military Technical Institute and let them try to find anything that would be false there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I am bringing this all into question because in your findings, you allegedly established that the shell was fired by the Serb side, although there were findings by UN experts that indicated that this came from the Muslim side. And although on the 15th of February the special team established that this was impossible.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
