utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you want to read my conclusion, and I have to say this to you, in my report it says quite clearly 18 degrees north north-east. The direction is there too. And also the angle is between 50 and 60 degrees.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sir, please.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Listen. Please listen. I listened to you, and I want to answer now. I said that there are six areas from where the projectile might have been fired, and this is on a military topographical map. And five of them -- there is one area that is on ABiH-controlled territory and five in Serb-controlled territory; nothing else. And that is my conclusion. So please do not put words into my mouth, especially not things that are not written in my report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, is it possible that all the UN experts who took part in the investigations, and none of them had any grounds for being partial, as opposed to you, how come they established something that was completely different? Because only your report established that it was fired from the Serb side. And you were the only one who had a direct interest in the results of the finding. You were the only one who was professional enough to establish that the shell was fired by the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know what to say to you, Mr. Milosevic. I never said anything derogatory about any UN report. I have never seen any one of them. There is nothing good or bad I can say about them. I first have to see these reports. I'm telling you for the umpteenth time that I have to see the report first. I don't know how professional they are and whether they are professional. But let me tell you, Mr. Milosevic, you will hardly find a person in -- anywhere in the world who worked on designing ammunition for 17 years and taught at university and was for three and a half years the target of projectiles and who had the opportunity of feeling himself what the combat effect of a projectile is. So I can tell you I have considerable experience, positive and negative. I know a lot of theoretical models that go into the phenomenon of fragmentation as far as projectiles are concerned, and I follow the research of American experts in this area. So I really am a good expert in this field. And as for the UN experts, I cannot say. I have told you very nicely, I've provided my report, you have my CV, and now you're telling me about some kind of experts that I never heard of, that I never read of. So I'm not quarreling about them. I never said anything about them, positive or negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not talking about them at all, sir. I'm talking about you. Isn't it evident that there is a conflict of interest that disqualifies you as an expert in this case because you were employed, attached to the General Staff of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina? You have a direct interest involved to have the Serbs blamed for this. Even in this professional expert report, you use derogatory terms for the Serbs. And for you, this -- this conflict of interest disqualifies you as an expert.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, way. Mr. Milosevic, when I wrote this report, I was not engaged by the military. That is one point. Secondly, the term "Chetnik" is not a derogatory term.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said "the aggressor side."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, yes. If somebody is throwing projectiles at me --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody -- did you target projectiles at them? There was the Sarajevo-Romanija Corps and there was the Bosnian Army Corps and there were two corps that were clashing. So didn't they exchange projectiles?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Rifle grenades with 150-metre range.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You say that you did not have artillery pieces.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm telling you what I did, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, Mr. Zecevic. But you know that the Serb positions were observed from other UN observation posts. And no firing of shells was observed from there either. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: How can I have that kind of information? I was an ordinary citizen in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. There is an UNPROFOR statement that it was impossible to establish who fired the shell, and you attach great importance to that. You only know of that statement. You don't know of any other statement of UNPROFOR, and you don't know about any other information provided by UNPROFOR. The only thing you know is that you don't know who fired the shell and that it is impossible to --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, if you read my report, I said that it was an announced over the radio, on the 6th, on the radio. It's not that I got a report. It was broadcast over the radio. The UN spokesperson said that from the positions of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina on that day - this can be checked - not a singe projectile was fired, and that is what my report says and nothing else. There is no special report that came to me from the UN.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. So you took from the UN only that which had to do with this statement that it was impossible. I hope that you're aware of the fact that the only report so far that claimed that the Serb side fired the shell is your report.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know that. I did not look at any other reports except for my own.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. I promised Mr. Tapuskovic to leave him 15 minutes, so I thank you, Mr. May.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank Mr. Milosevic too. Your Honours, I would like to put a few things to the witness, things that he stated and documents that he alone used when providing his findings.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So, Mr. Witness, I would like to start with the statement that you gave on the 13th of December or, rather, in July of the -- to the investigators of the Tribunal. It's a lengthy statement. I'm interested in only one paragraph. It is paragraph 37 of that statement of yours. Let me show you what you said there, please. Mr. Zecevic, please look at paragraph 37. You say here, and I am reading this now so that you wouldn't have to read it. "From April/May 1993, mortar shells and projectiles that were fired by the Serb side against Sarajevo were manufactured in Serbia. I know that because from August 1992, I had introduced the practice of collecting unexploded mines and projectiles, and the -- so that the explosives taken out of them could be used for the needs of the army of BH." Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "Furthermore, I was looking for volunteers --" so you were a volunteer too; right? "-- to go around Sarajevo to collect these unexploded explosive devices." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: "That was practice which, in normal circumstances, would not be carried out, but since the government forces had a critical lack of weaponry, there was no alternative." And then you used "...each and every kilogramme of explosives to make..." and so and so forth.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Ten rifle grenades.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Ten rifle grenades. Never mind. But what I'm interested in is that you collected these unexploded explosive devices; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Logically.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And one sentence further down you say: "This was customary practice in Yugoslavia, namely these explosive devices that were brought to me by people had their manufacturer's name and the year of manufacture marked"; is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you were collecting these bodies of the projectiles, and you had them among your own weaponry.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. We just used the explosives, because nobody would be crazy enough to put into a mortar the body of a mortar shell that had already been fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. But in your statement of the 7th of September, I will show you if necessary --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Please do show it to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Here it is. I'm have to show it to you again. Here it is. Again, it was given to the investigators. You say here in paragraph 7, the one but last paragraph, that you and Sarajevo made shells at Alipasino Polje, the foundry there?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Not I.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Was this done under your control?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Under my control it was only hand grenades and rifle grenades that were made. This was done by the Pretis factory, but it did not fall under me. I was a military unit and they were an economic entity.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Now look at the statement that you received today and that was presented to the Judges awhile ago. Mr. Milosevic showed it to you a few minutes ago too. It has to do with what you said were the security services centre. You said that you did not ask them for anything, but I am reading your statement of the 26th and 27th of February 1996 to you. On page 1 in the middle you say: "I decided to establish contact with the security services centre and to ask them whether I could conduct an investigation in this respects. They agreed." So it was not expertise you sought?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, wait a minute. I have to have a look at this. I cannot say anything. Give me the page number, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Here it is, and it was underlined as a matter of fact. It had already been presented to the Judges. Here it is on page 1. Page 1, paragraph 7. You said quite literally what I said to you. "I contacted the security service centre and asked if it was possible for me to conduct an investigation." So you were conducting an investigation. You were not giving an expert opinion.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no. Wait a minute. It was a judge who engaged me. They just made it possible for me to come to the site.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Did you state what it says here in this statement or not?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Look, I cannot conduct an investigation within the centre when I'm not a member of the security centre -- services.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But that's what you said.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's a mistranslation.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Look at what you said: "I did not agree with the opinion of General Smith because there is a difference in shells used by the Chetniks and by the ABiH. The shells produced in Sarajevo were not made of wrought steel but from pieces of steel or cast steel." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: This is, again, a misinterpretation. I used a different word, a different kind of iron.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Wait a minute. You corrected it later in your September from -- in your September statement you say, on page 1 in paragraph 4 --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It's steel.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: This is what you said in 1996, that it wasn't made of -- now how did you put it. That it wasn't made of wrought steel.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: But made of cast steel. That is what you said. Of pieces of steel, not of wrought steel. Would you like to explain it to the Judges?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Because of technological differences, because there were no presses, et cetera, a number of projectiles, not in my unit but at the Pretis factory in Sarajevo, so I did not take part in this, I just know about it, I have nothing to do with it, they would use a block of steel and then they would mechanically cut this steel, and they would make mines out of it. Afterwards, they managed to develop their own technology of founding -- casting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So in September 2000, you corrected yourself.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No, no, I did not correct myself. It's the very same thing. For a technical person, it's the very same thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please, look at what you said in paragraph 4 of your statement in September.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: It is not contradictory.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Please explain it to the Judges.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you what to explain to the judges.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, I've put the question to you. I always seem to be in a hurry because the time, and I know I'm speaking too fast. So I'm reading this: "In relation to this statement made previously, shells made in Sarajevo were not made of wrought steel but from pieces of steel or cast steel."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I've just tried to explain this to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Well, please hear me out. Please hear me out so that you could give the Judges the explanation that is necessary. And you say: "My sentence was not interpreted properly. Shells of the BH army were made of cast iron, rolled iron." So did you understand that you had made a mistake and that you wanted to correct it when you saw what the shell had been made from?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Distinguished colleague, have you seen my report? There is no reference in it whatsoever what kind of steel it is, cast or rolled. The question here had to do with external ballistics, determining the locality. If you look at my report, no reference is made to pieces of steel. What the Prosecution asked me about was whether I as an expert could explain to them how the development of ammunition manufacturing went in Sarajevo. That is what I said in my statement to them. But in my expert report, there is no reference absolutely to any technologies that were involved in this. I did not call them -- I did not analyse these pieces. I analysed the external ballistics of the projectile and the stabiliser. So for this expert opinion, this is totally insignificant. Why would it be significant whether the material was cast or rolled? And whether the pieces will be in the shape of a blade or irregular shapes, if a projectile is --

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, we don't have time for this.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if you have time or not. Now because you do not have time you are going to bring me in a position that would make it seem that I stated something that I didn't state.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say that as opposed to what Smith found.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. Well, his first statement was that the projectile did not have a fuse.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: We will have to go back to the absolute core of the matter. In item 2 of your conclusions --

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Just a moment. Let me find the conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: You say: "There is no possibility of an explosion caused by a stationary explosive device."

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And in the statement you have before you, the one given in September, look at the penultimate paragraph. You said: Professor Zecevic handed over to the team of investigators a photocopy of the report of the Serb expert, Miroljub Vukasinovic, in which he speaks about the mortar action in Markale in Sarajevo." And look at the last sentence now: "Professor Zecevic said that although these are two different incidents, the information from the reports are relevant to the incident that occurred on the 5th of February, 1994." From the Office of the Prosecutor, I got this -- these findings that you handed over to the OTP. I believe that it is relevant, and I would like to indicate something in it to you. What is stated in para 2, does it mean that you are in fact contesting the contents of this report you yourself submitted to the investigators?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Where are you exactly?

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: And this is consistent with what you said about the angle: "The analysis made of the position of the crater, the place of impact, the angle of the stabiliser, and the numerical measurements of impact on the target, it can be concluded on this basis that the shell fell under static conditions under an angle of 55 to 60 degrees." That is precisely the angle that you spoke about all the time. They seem to be identical. What can you tell us about this finding? Is it relevant?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I hold Mr. Vukasinovic in high esteem. He is a good expert but he has no practical experience. He is a good expert when it comes to simulations. This whole theory is based on very good concepts. But in my whole report, I never say that I accepted his conclusions. You cannot call these conclusions identical. I said, however, that the methodology of Mr. Vukasinovic is interesting. Is can be debated opinion. And we have other pieces of information here. But generally speaking, it is an interesting concept that can be usefully involved in analysis. However, the report of Mr. Vukasinovic is useful because it provides one possible concept: He tried to explain this phenomenon. He did not explain it in fact, because he made several errors, but this is not important for our case.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: So you accept it from that point of view?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: No. You cannot have me say what I never meant to say. People from the Prosecution asked me what can be done. I told them here is the report of Mr. Vukasinovic, he is a good expert, a young man whom I respect, his conclusions are not completely correct, but his theory is not unfounded, and some concepts from his theory I used in my own analysis. And it says in my expert opinion given to the Prosecution that I did not accept his conclusions, I just said that his theory was interesting.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: What I'm interested in and what you have to explain to the Judges concerns this angle. If it -- we are talking about a statical instrument, the angle established is consistent with the one that you measured, not the angle measured by the UN investigation team.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Look, the angle has nothing to do with it. When you fire a projectile, depending on the distance, on the angle of elevation, you will have completely different angles. To make this clearer, I will show you this example. Here is a mortar. It's important for understanding what angles are all about. This 55 angle has nothing to do with Markale 1994. Markale 1994 and 1995 are two different cases. This is the mortar from which the projectile was fired. It can change elevation from 45 to 65 degrees. The shell has additional charges. The more charges inside, the higher the velocity of firing. Now, take two teams. Take two crews and give them the task of firing from two different positions, two different shells --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. Time is rather against us.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one more question, please, if I can complete my examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. TAPUSKOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, what is interesting is that the radars operated by the representatives of the international community did not record the firing of any rockets, and there are no witnesses who seem to have seen them. Radars did not register the -- any rockets flying over the area where the projectile was supposed to have been fired over. How can you explain this? Because you say in your report that a projectile can be seen by the naked eye.

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: First of all, a mortar shell is not the same as projectile. Second, the radars were positioned in the Sarajevo airport, and they were not turned on. Therefore, the projectile that flew in was completely on the opposite side in relation to the radars. So that doesn't mean anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We are going to finish now. Thank you very much. Yes. I'm afraid that's going to include --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please wait a minute. It's not clear to me. It's about the raw material of the shell. Is it true, as you suggested in your statement in 1996, there is a difference in shells used by the Serbs and by the Bosnian army?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: The difference was in the quality of material used for the body of the projectile. They had presses and could manufacture the body --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That being the case, apart from the analysis of ballistics of projectile, why did you not analyse the fragments found in the Markale place at that time?

utterances.speaker: BERKO ZECEVIC
utterances.text: They were completely irrelevant to determining the position of the origin of fire. Fragments are important if you want to establish how many people could have been killed. One mortar shell had 3 to 5.000 fragments that fly at a speed of 1.000 to 1.500 metres/second. They are important to ballistic experts, not to somebody trying to find the origin of fire. What mattered to me was the stabiliser fin and the point of firing. On the basis of that, you could draw certain conclusions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, if there's no time for re-examine could I at least ask that the photographs that we used in cross-examination be exhibited.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And they can be included. And we should exhibit the Defence Exhibit also later.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will deal with that next week formally. Yes, Mr. Nice, we've really got to end, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I cut across the evidence simply to say this. The project on showing relevance of the intercepts that we seek to have admitted has been completed. Files are available for you now. This deals with the Bosnian intercepts which have been reduced to what the Prosecution has reduced to a minimum, every one being relevant but they've been grouped two ways for your assistance. First chronologically with themes identified. The themes are then set out, and then the intercepts have been regrouped according to the themes so that you can see them in that context. A list of dramatis personae is added at the end. There are three more potential intercept collections all much smaller than this, two of them depending on decisions about particular witnesses, either identified or being identified by, amongst others, the Prosecutor. At least one and probably two of those fall for collation in a similar way. There's a final collection of intercepts which would be admitted in an entirely different way and probably wouldn't merit this particular form of collation. But the project has been completed by, as I indicated, the in-house expert, together with others of the team who are identified on the footer of the first page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. We are grateful, and you are now free to go.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We will adjourn now until next Tuesday.
